speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ACCRA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether he has now received the texts of the speeches made at the commonwealth meeting in Accra by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: ACCRA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
I have received a copy of the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I have not yet received those of the Minister of Finance. I think it would be most appropriate that as soon as they return an opportunity should be given for them to place before the house what they said.
I may say in this connection, having tabled the full text of the communique, that reading the communique will, I think, put in proper perspective the statements that were made. The strongest guarantee of the future of the commonwealth is its capacity to face the facts in a straightforward manner and to do something about them. The various commonwealth members spoke very freely about the situation. Indeed, the frank views put forward by Canada and the other members of the commonwealth did not in any way seem to have been considered out of place by the United Kingdom.
I might point out in this connection that Mr. Maudling is reported to have implied in London on his return from Accra that after the preliminary discussions had taken
place, or words to this effect, then consideration would be given to the convening of a prime ministers' conference. I want to get the exact words of the press report:
The meeting had shown considerable support for a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers.
And Mr. Maudling is quoted as saying:
I think it is very likely that there will be one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ACCRA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. While I thank the Prime Minister for tabling the communique, is the Prime Minister aware that the chancellor of the exchequer, who was the head of the U.K. delegation at Accra, said the other day that he did not feel the communique itself fully represented the tenor of the discussions at that meeting; and is that not an additional reason why the texts of the speeches in so far as we are able to secure them should be tabled?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: ACCRA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORTED STATEMENTS BY CANADIAN MINISTERS
speechtext:
I can only say that in the communique-and communiques are always accepted by all those who participate- these words appear, and I think they are the answer to the Leader of the Opposition:
Paragraph 7: Representatives of the United Kingdom reviewed the various reasons that had led them to make the application.
Paragraph 8: All other commonwealth representatives expressed grave apprehension and concern regarding the possible results of the initiative taken by the United Kingdom. They reaffirmed the value and importance they attach to traditional commonwealth trading arrangements under which most foodstuffs, raw materials and manufactures enter the United Kingdom free of duty from commonwealth countries with, in most cases, preferential advantages; and other commonwealth countries make reciprocal tariff concessions. The benefits of these arrangements accrue to the United Kingdom as well as to other commonwealth countries.
Then comes paragraph 9:
Most commonwealth countries questioned whether the United Kingdom with its other international and domestic obligations could possibly secure in the proposed negotiations an agreement which would protect commonwealth interests adequately and effectively.
I think a general reading of the communique-I have not picked out selected portions-would indicate that there was a high degree of unanimity among the countries represented at this conference, pointing out the serious difficulties which entry into the common market might have not only on the economics of the commonwealth but also on its political constitution.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, senior officers who accept public speaking engagements in which they deal with general defence policy are requested to submit the text of their speech to me prior to delivery.
Air Marshal Slemon appeared with General Kuter, the commander of NOR AD, on an A.B.C. television network program entitled "Issues and Answers" on September 10. The program was one of a series of public affairs presentations by the American Broadcasting Company and dealt with the functioning of the NORAD combat operation centre.
The questions addressed to Air Marshal Slemon were in general factual and the answers given contained material previously approved and in no way dealt with our defence policy as a whole. Air Marshal Slemon did comment on the recent tracking of the Russian space shot containing Major Titof and stated the fact that the astronaut crossed over Canada a number of times in his earth orbits. Air Marshal Slemon stressed the fact that it was of the utmost importance that we should be able to keep track of such flights, and he stated the opinion that this required a maximum effort on the part of NORAD.
I am entirely satisfied that it was quite unnecessary in this case to obtain my prior approval and permission.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State. Has the minister any comment to make regarding the statements made by Messrs. C. A. Faucher and Roger Perri, former members of the Quebec liquor board police, who stated in court recently that they performed political work in the constituency of Bellechasse during the federal election of 1958?

maintopic: REPORTED IRREGULARITIES RESPECTING ELECTION OF SECRETARY OF STATE

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: REPORTED IRREGULARITIES RESPECTING ELECTION OF SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though I think this question is out of order, I am glad that it was put to me. This is how the presiding judge, Mr. Justice Pettigrew, cleared up the matter yesterday morning, September 18, 1961:
The court: during the week end, my attention was drawn to a Montreal newspaper report concerning the testimony of a former Quebec liquor board police member, C. R. Faucher, of Rimouski. That was at the sitting of Friday, September 15, during the Lemire investigation.
Sunday morning, after mass, I got a copy of that newspaper and I asked the stenographer to transcribe Faucher's testimony for me. Here is one of the questions the crown attorney, Mr. Bienvenu, asked him: "While you were a member of the liquor board police force and especially since 1951 and 1952, did you ever participate in election campaigns?"
Answer: Participated-that is in 1957-
The court: I insist on this date, 1957, and the witness continued:	"In 1957, that is before	thefederal elections. I	was sent on	a trip	in Bellechasse. Mr. Cote called me in and told me: You will meet doctor Poirier in St. Damien. Put yourself at his disposal. He said that you were to meet him there. Pick up a certain nurse by the name of Normandin in front of the Chateau Frontenac and go to the hotel where the doctor lives in St. Damien de Bellechasse. The next morning, the doctor told me that the only thing I had to do was	to drive the	nurse	who	waswith me. She was	going to the	health	units	run
by the nuns-

The court: Other questions by Mr. Bienvenu.
Question: If it was not an election campaign.
Answer: She went to give some medical aid She told me, when the trip was over, that she had gone to see the sisters to get their vote for Mr. Dorion. I just say what she told me I did not go in with her. End of the answer.
The judge continues and I am still quoting from the shorthand notes:
"And I, as judge, immediately stated, as it was my duty to do, that such evidence was only hearsay, that such proof was illegal, and I added that the nurse had to come herself to give evidence in that connection.
Now this newspaper states the following, and the judge quotes:
"A witness gave evidence in the court of the sessions of the peace yesterday according to Saturday's newspaper during an investigation with regard to the former liquor police chief Rosario Lemire in the 1958 election."
By the court: That fact is not correct.
And the judge continues the quotation:
"And the reverend sisters of the religious orders of Bellechasse had been solicited to vote for the Progressive Conservative candidate, Mr. Noel Dorion."
By the court: What is inaccurate, it is the year 1958. You are aware of the fact that a question of justice is involved, as I have said, and as I say again: the judge is not a partisan for one side or the other. I am here simply to discharge my duty, to see that justice is done, and that my inquiry is carried on in a legal manner.
Now I blame this newspaper for having mentioned 1958. Was it deliberate? Was it done by in-advertance? The witness did not say 1958, he said 1957. Now, in 1957, Mir. Dorion was not a candidate in the Bellechasse riding. I mention here, and it is public knowledge, that when he was elected it was the first time and it was in 1958.
And the newspaper printed a large enough heading for its report.
And the judge quotes:
"Nuns urged to vote for Mr. Dorion". This, despite the fact that I have declared that such evidence was illegal and only hearsay. The newspaper could have mentioned the evidence given by the witness but it should have added that such evidence was of such a nature that the judge could not take it into account. And you know that when someone occupies a position such as Mr. Dorion's who is a federal minister, such statements are liable to cause him rather considerable prejudice ... I thought I had to make a rectification, 1 don't know if we can call it that, but this goes to show you that we want justice for everyone and if, by any chance, it happens that something is reported inadvertently that is not quite in order, and would be of such a nature as to cause prejudice to a private individual, I should make the same remarks I just made in connection with Mr. Dorion. I would do the same for a labourer and for a tradesman.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked me whether the request by Mr. Whitfield for permission to prosecute under the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act has been granted. subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ALLEGED SUPPRESSION OF RELIGIOUS RIGHTS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont asked me a question, as follows:

Will the Prime Minister inform the house whether the government has sent or will send a protest to the Cuban government against the suppression of religious rights and freedom, indicated by the dismissal of a number of the clergy?
The Canadian embassy in Cuba has now confirmed that nine Canadians were among the Roman Catholic priests expelled from Cuba, who sailed on Sunday night for Spain on board a Spanish vessel. Neither the Canadian ambassador nor the Canadian consul was able to obtain permission to visit the Canadian missionaries before their forced departure. The Canadian ambassador secured an interview with the acting minister of foreign affairs yesterday, in the course of which he expressed the Canadian government's concern over the arbitrary deportation of Canadian citizens to a third country without any notification or explanation, in a manner so precipitate as to deny them an opportunity to make even a minimum of personal arrangements or to communicate with the embassy.
A further report on these representations is expected today, and when this is received I shall inform the house of any further developments in this very regrettable incident.

Now that we are discussing this bill on second reading I have two ideas which I should like to put forward. It seems to me that this centennial celebration will provide us with an opportunity which we have not had for a hundred years, and which we may not have again for another hundred years, to take a great leap forward in building national unity. Unity is the strength of every nation, and should be the prime goal of our national development. If we are to achieve complete national unity it seems to me that we must learn to appreciate one another, and learn to appreciate the contributions which the various provinces have made to Canada as a nation in addition to the contributions which the various racial groups have made to our culture and our economy.
Yesterday the Prime Minister put forward the idea of a train which could travel from one part of Canada to another carrying visible tokens of our heritage. I think that is an excellent idea, and I should like to see it developed to the point where the Prime Minister or those responsible for organizing that train would see to it that prominently displayed were exhibits making it clear what have been the contributions of each province and each ethnic group.
As reported at the bottom of page 8467 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
As Canada is a country on the threshold of an exciting tomorrow, the centenary should serve as a launching pad for new triumphs in our second century.
Earlier in the debate he recalled that this should also be a time of national stocktaking and of rededication to the future. In this connection I should like to put forward the idea that it also affords a splendid opportunity for establishing minimum standards of public service for all Canadians. This would probably mean setting up another committee to determine suitable standards. I do not think the task of such a committee would be an impossible one. We have, for example, already agreed on certain standards of health, so many hospital beds for each thousand people, and I think if we started from there and worked out, say, miles of paved roads, per thousand people, standards of education-so many classrooms per thousand students-and so on we should have the minimum standards which we could make our goal for all Canadians during the next hundred years.
This does not mean that everyone would have to be pulled down to the common level, but I think if those standards were determined Canadians would be shocked to see what wide

variations exist as between one part of Canada and another, and even between different parts of the same province. I think this is something we would want to eradicate in the course of the next hundred years, and I hope the Prime Minister will consider setting up a committee under this legislation to determine suitable minimum standards of public service which might be made common for all Canada, and which might be the goals toward which we can work in the future.

A few days ago I was in Toronto, and there I saw a motion picture called "Windjammer" which recorded a cruise of the Norwegian training ship Christian Raadich. I was impressed by the fact that after watching that film for two hours one almost wished to be Norwegian. The Prime Minister has frequently referred to the richness of the ethnic groups we find in this country, and I think he prides himself on the leadership he has taken in bringing this heritage to the fore. Certainly our former governor general did a great deal in this direction.
It seems to me that if the national film board could plan ahead and produce a great motion picture accompanied by original Canadian music by some of our finest composers, a picture which would introduce our Eskimo population, our native Indians and all the other ethnic groups we have in this country, a significant contribution would have been made toward the celebration. Such a fdm would include our old pioneer stock as well as the people who have come recently from Europe bringing with them so many colourful traditions and customs. It would also include passages illustrating our varied scenery; I have in mind the thousand islands region, the Rockies and other Canadian scenes. A picture of this kind would present Canada to every country in the world, and we could afford to export copies free for distribution abroad.

I speak briefly with respect to a view which has been expressed by many individuals in my riding. It is a view which is shared not only by many who were born in my riding but by others who have since come there to live. As is known to most hon. members, Niagara Falls is one of the most popular tourist areas of the country. Not so well known, however, is the fact that this area has rich historical associations. In and about the area from

Niagara Falls to Fort Erie were fought battles as significant in their way as the battle of the plains of Abraham.
I think no Canadian who has visited Quebec City can fail to be stirred by the magnificent monuments there to the two fine peoples who were the founders of this country. The peace, the dignity and the beauty of the surroundings, wedded to the recollection of all we have been taught about the battle which there took place, cannot fail to be impressive. Anyone visiting that spot would feel the beginnings of Canada.
I suggest that the same should be true in Niagara, where there was a struggle between forces from the south who sought to have that part of Canada made part of the United States, and the British troops, Canadian militiamen, the Canadian people who had settled in that area and the Indians of our country who remained loyal to the crown. Unhappily some of the great battles which were fought there, such as the battle of Lundy's lane, have never been properly commemorated by a national park. In fact, in Niagara Falls there are only a small monument and some poignant graves of the fallen on both sides. Each year there has been a commemorative service. Until recently it was held only by Canadians but two years ago, for the first time, Americans were asked to participate. Last year, for the first time in 157 years, an American was asked to give the address.
This is, historians agree, one of the bloodiest battlegrounds on the North American continent. It has been said by historians that more blood was shed on that land, proportionate to the size of the population and the number engaged in the struggle, than was shed at Gettysburg. Most hon. members have visited Gettysburg and will know the feeling that comes to one when visiting there, a sense of seeing the roots of that country's struggle for existence.
It is unhappily the fact that the area which comprises the Lundy's lane battle ground is largely built over with commercial establishments and two fine churches. There is virtually nothing to remind either the residents of the area or the millions of visitors who come to that part of the country that here a stand was made for freedom, and that that part of Canada was held for what later became this great dominion.
I urge upon those who are to serve on this commission the need to commemorate in a tangible way some of the great battles that have significance to Canadians in our emergence as a nation, with a view to paying a tribute in this way to those who went before us, and reminding all who come after us of

the beginnings of our nation when we celebrate its hundredth birthday a few years hence.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to follow along the same line as what was said by the hon. member for Niagara Falls, and to bring to the attention of the house some historical facts pertaining to the area I represent.
I heartily support the Prime Minister's bill to establish a commission to ensure that Canada's centennial will be properly celebrated. As we look to the future toward a greater Canada for those who will follow us, it is important that we pause to look at our past and examine what has been done in days gone by which laid the foundation for the greatness Canada has achieved as a nation today.
In my riding there is the old town of Niagara-on-the-Lake, where the first government of Upper Canada was established many years ago. It also played an important role in the defence of Upper Canada during the war of 1812. In that town today we have several fine churches, some of them dating back to those early days. We also have Fort Missis-sagi and a number of other old, historic buildings. We have in that area the makings of a splendid old colonial town similar to Jamestown in the United States if it were properly preserved, which I think it should be.
As recently as Sunday last I attended a ceremony at Niagara-on-the-Lake to unveil a plaque in memory of Colonel John Butler, who formed Butler Rangers who played a great part in the preservation of the Niagara peninsula as part of Canada. They also did outstanding work at the time of the American revolution in piloting refugees from the United States to Canada. We therefore have in the Niagara peninsula an historic town and many fine old buildings. As part of our centennial preparations across Canada leading to our celebration we should give serious thought to preserving for posterity what is left of those early, trying times.
It is true that the Ontario government through the Niagara parks commission has done a great deal to preserve places of historic importance in the Niagara peninsula, but there is a great deal more to be done. At the Niagara camp training grounds there are approximately 900 acres of land much of which is going to waste at this time. With that amount of land and the buildings I mentioned the remains of a colonial town could be preserved to commemorate those stirring days in Canada's early history. I urge the Prime Minister and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to give serious

Canadian Centennial
consideration to preserving what remains of the historic colonial days in the Niagara peninsula.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AMOUNTS AVAILABLE FOR LOANS AND RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was saying that one of the first results of the fiscal policy of this government was to increase interest rates. The government should now try to reduce them, particularly for housing. If and when the government takes such action there will be, of course, thousands of Canadian home buyers left holding the bag with blanket mortgages on their homes bearing an interest rate of 6J

per cent. Their homes will not be readily saleable because cheaper mortgages will be available at such a time.
Yesterday the Minister of Public Works praised the 6f per cent 35 year mortgage. He said that not too many of them had been taken. Just imagine what a 35 year mortgage means to a man who takes it when he is a little over 30 years of age. If he is fortunate enough not to fall ill or encounter other misfortunes he may be lucky enough to have it paid off before he reaches the allotted span of three score years and ten. The old age pension might be used to finish paying it off, but if he does not live some member of his family will have to pick up the tab and continue the payments. If the owner of one of these houses bothers to add up the amount of money he has paid over the years he will find that he has paid about twice its original value. He then owns an old house by the time the mortgage is discharged. This problem is brought about by the high interest rate of 6J per cent. The point is that interest rates should not be so high as to require a 35 year mortgage on any house.
Recently I saw an advertisement in a Montreal newspaper which offered for sale a nine year old house with a mortgage that bore an interest rate of only 5i per cent. The 5J per cent interest rate caught my eye, because I can recall some years ago in this house the Minister of Finance and other hon. members of the Conservative party berating the former government on the ground that 5J per cent was an unjustifiably high interest rate for housing.
The Minister of Public Works always seems happy to announce a large number of housing starts. This means that a great many more buyers are caught in the trap of paying high interest rates over the years. Certainly long after this government has been gone-but not easily forgotten-many thousands of Canadians will continue to pay monthly tribute to its memory, and the home purchasers will be in the vanguard of that throng.
Another feature of high interest rates on mortgages is this. After a man has put his name on the dotted line and purchased a home this tends to keep him put, to render him immobile. He is frozen in one position, and in all likelihood will continue to live in the same house on the same street in the same town for the rest of his life, unless he is willing to sell at a financial loss. That is not so true in the early years when he only has the down payment as an equity, but as the equity builds up it is more difficult to dispose of the house, to find a buyer with a sufficient amount of money to enable the
National Housing Act
original purchaser to recover his down payment and his equity in the building. As I have said, this equity is difficult to finance under the present system. The trouble is that at the present time buyers do not have sufficient money to finance this equity, so they are forced to buy a new house under a mortgage bearing an interest rate of 6f per cent.
Another problem is that some areas are overbuilt. I know of some areas containing empty homes that would be suitable for anyone who wished to buy, yet other homes are being built under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation financing and these entail mortgages bearing an interest rate of 6f per cent, all because of the lower down payment.
The question of financing the equity in older homes should be given consideration by the government. Under the present system of financing we do not make the best use of existing houses. I have known several people who have been required to move, sometimes to another town some distance away, because of a job transfer. I have known people who required a larger house because of an increase in the size of their family. These people have been unable to derive from their homes a sufficient equity to purchase new homes. The government should give consideration to this and other related problems. I am in favour of the government advancing money for housing, but it should be made available at lower interest rates.
The hon. member for Nipissing said yesterday that during the last year of office of the previous administration there were 380,000 housing starts, and that only $65 million was taken from the public sector, the rest being taken from the private sector. I have heard the Prime Minister say that his party was for free enterprise. Well, the public sector of the economy has put up $924 million in order to finance only 30,000 more starts. The private sector of the economy has been treated well by the Minister of Finance. Government securities reached a high price and this lessened the interest of investors in housing mortgages. In order to provide our people with enough money to build houses the government was forced to put a great deal of money into these projects. They now provide those long term mortgage loans by borrowing on the short side of the market. Most of the money required for the long term mortgages is constantly being churned about in the short term market, and this costs a lot of money. This is the main reason mortgage money is at 6J per cent today.
When he replies the minister might give us some figures on the repossession of houses by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and by any other agency holding mortgages

National Housing Act
guaranteed by the government. It would be interesting to have those figures, particularly in respect of the length of occupancy on the part of the house owners.
Yesterday the minister referred to the money advanced in connection with sewage treatment projects on the part of the municipalities. I know some of those projects have gone ahead. I agree that we should clean up our lakes and rivers; I think it is a very good thing. At that time the minister said that money would be advanced to the municipalities at a price very little above the cost to the government. I ask the minister now how much money has been advanced to the municipalities, and what interest rate is being charged.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find the first clause of the bill before us very interesting, and this applies particularly to the residents of northern Manitoba, the area which I have the honour to represent. There are one or two things that I should like to point out. However, at the outset I should like to say that congratulations to the minister and to this government are certainly in order for the tremendous interest they have shown in housing requirements over the last four years. Each year we have seen increases in the amount of money available for house building, and I think I would be quite safe in saying that new records in house building in Canada have been set in three of the last four years.
However, there are one or two problems remaining in regard to money available from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the National Housing Act. In this respect I should like to bring two matters to the attention of the minister. First of all, I am quite interested in clause 1 of the bill, the purpose of which is to increase from $1.5 billion to $2 billion the maximum charge on the consolidated revenue fund for direct lending by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I know from experience that one area of Canada is handicapped to a great extent in its desire to get approval of those loans by individual home owners. I refer particularly to the new area in Manitoba known as Thompson, which is the site of the new International Nickel development. I am sure the minister is aware of this situation because I brought it to his attention previously.
When house construction started at Thompson, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation lent money to individual applicants provided, of course, that the International Nickel Company guaranteed those loans. Until recent months this worked out fairly satisfactorily, because most of the people going into that area were employed by International Nickel, and the mining company was

not at all reluctant to guarantee those loans. However, since then the town has developed rapidly and people are moving in to supply the goods and services which are necessary in a town of this size. They are anxious to build houses, but they are not on the payroll of the mining company. The mining company is now reluctant to guarantee loans for anyone other than its own employees.
As I say, I am sure the minister is aware of this, but owing to the tremendous development in Thompson and other places in the north I think a special look should be taken at this problem and special consideration should be given to those areas. At Thompson there is every reason why we should have faith in the future of the development. When you see an individual company go into an area and invest possibly up to $200 million of its own money to build the first fully integrated nickel producing plant in the world and supply the services for a well planned town, schools and things of that sort; when you see this followed up by private enterprise in the form of small industry, shopping centres and all the requirements for a well planned town go in, I think there is every assurance that this industry will be located in that area for a long period of time. I can recall the president of the company, Mr. Gordon of New York, saying at the opening that as far as they were concerned they intended to remain in that area forever. The establishments which have been put up certainly bear out the fact that they intend to stay for a long time.
If we are to fully justify our faith in the north and our plans to develop the north, special consideration should be given to places such as this and to the private individual who wishes to go in and build a home for himself and his family. I also believe that when you see a town of 400 to 500 houses built in the last year and a half, with another 200 or 300 houses under construction at the present time and something in the neighbourhood of 500 to 600 new lots opening up next year, this certainly warrants greater consideration from the department and from Central Mortgage and Housing than is now being shown.
I realize, of course, that some sad experiences have developed in the past in certain one industry towns. However, as I said before, if we are going to justify our faith in the north I think special consideration should be given. I say this because not only this government but governments of the past have more or less gone on record as having faith in the north and have recognized the need to show special consideration through

the northern allowances which they have paid to government employees stationed in the north.
Many people who go there find that building costs are greater than in any other part of Canada. I might say at this time that I understand Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has experienced some difficulty in these areas because of permafrost. I know that at the present time officials of the national research council are looking into this factor to see what other types of buildings might be more desirable in these localities. However, in the case of Thompson I understand that only eight or nine out of the 450 to 500 houses that have been built are more or less coming apart at the seams as the result of permafrost. In only eight or nine cases has the sad misfortune occurred of running into trouble because of permafrost.
There are other such places in the north in each of our provinces, and there are localities in my area other than Thompson which are having difficulty in getting loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation simply because I believe it is considered that a one industry community is perhaps not the best place to invest too much money. However, in listening to the hon. member for Welland I noticed he said that in his area houses were very difficult to sell from the point of view of the owner getting his equity out of the sale. I think the situation not only applies to the north but possibly applies to many other parts of Canada. Some of these other parts of Canada are not experiencing difficulty in getting loans. Therefore I respectfully request the minister to ask the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to take a further look at these communities in the north and give the fullest possible consideration to a loosening of their policy to allow the individual home owner to secure a loan through these facilities.

National Housing Act
what is the future of this development if it continues in the direction and to the extent that it has in the past months and years? Often the question is asked, if I bought a home for $15,000 what would it be worth five years from now? There is a very useful study of housing contained in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, September 16 last under the title "Renting or Buying? How Costs Compare". I should like to read one short paragraph from the article:
An $800 down payment is needed under the National Housing Act to purchase that $15,000 house. Your monthly mortgage payments, including mortgage insurance fee, will amount to $97.97. Add $700 a year ($58.33) for taxes and maintenance costs. This makes your total monthly payments $156.30. By 1986 these payments have amounted to $46,890 to pay for and maintain that $15,000 bungalow.
The writer of the article indicates that the house buyer at the present time would be paying more by buying a home than he would by renting, projected over a 25 year period. At the end of that period, of course, he has the house. In the other case he has not risked the investment of $15,000 and he has nothing but the next month's rent to pay. It is also indicated in an article on the same page that on the average a house constructed under the National Housing Act today costs the buyer $1,012 more than the $13,366 it cost in 1956. The conclusion appears to be evident from the study that home prices are remaining stable but the value of money is changing.
I simply leave this word of caution with the house. We know that in our smaller towns and cities it is extremely difficult to sell real estate today even if it is very highly mortgaged and requires only a small equity to transfer a property. While there is much reason, of course, to assist people who need homes, I hope that the minister, with his wise and broad knowledge of the law to which he sometimes refers, will bear in mind the implications of this projection. Certainly this does not sound like private enterprise to me.

Mr. Speaker, I have very few remarks to make, but I do want to express my support for this measure, which increases the funds available for housing in general, university buildings, assistance to municipalities in connection with sewage disposal and for research. I am sure that the measure has the support of all members of the house.
However, I wish to make one or two suggestions. First of all I wish to support the representations of the hon. member for Welland with respect to the necessity of a reduction in interest rates. If one reads the history of housing in most western countries throughout the years, one will find that in relation to the interest rates in many other countries, ours is an extremely high rate of interest. If it is not feasible at the present time, I would ask the minister when he replies later to tell us whether consideration is being given to the provision of better homes for persons below a certain income by applying some bonus or write-off system, such as that which has been so successful under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act. Good housing is essential in order to build good communities and a strong nation. I think we would be fully justified in extending a write-off provision, similar to that under the small holdings section of the Veterans' Land Act, to those building houses for their families below a certain income level and below a certain house cost level.
I should like the minister to say whether any consideration is being given to that matter. I think the state is fully justified in subsidizing that type of housing in order to meet that type of need. We subsidize a good many other things which I believe are not as essential or as urgent as housing.
In view of the response we have had from municipalities in my constituency, and conversations which I have had with others, I suggest that the present regulations with respect to loans for the building of sewage disposal facilities are rather stringent, in that they apply only to main trunk line sewers and things of that sort. Those regulations might be quite satisfactory for the cities or the towns and larger municipalities. However, owing to the nature of the installations, I have been informed that the regulations are somewhat too restrictive to allow smaller municipalities, especially incorporated villages to take full advantage of the act. I would ask the minister when he replies to tell us whether consideration is being given to changing the regulations, in view of the representations made by various municipalities and organizations.
Then I just wish to say a word or two about the promotion of more building in the

smaller communities. There has been more of it in recent years. At this point I might say that I have no criticism to offer of the senior officials or local officials. Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on one clause on this bill, namely the clause which provides for loans to build dormitories for students at universities. I think this is an extremely important addition to the National Housing Act regulations, which was brought into effect last year and which apparently is going over very well.
At the time the regulations were brought into effect last year I raised the matter of loans for the building of dormitories for student nurses, graduate nurses, hospital aides and interns in hospitals. I have been associated with the board of governors of our hospital for a good many years, and I am well aware of all the problems in connection with getting funds to provide these facilities. Perhaps the minister has had no call for that kind of assistance; however, I feel that it is an extremely important matter.
It is true that both the federal government and the provincial government make available grants for building dormitories for student nurses. However, there is nothing in the way of loans for accommodation for graduate nurses, and the grants for accommodation for student nurses fall far short of the money that is required. In the newspapers the other day I noticed a statement to the effect that graduate nurses stood about lowest, in the matter of average income, of most professional people. That is a very unfortunate situation, because they also require good accommodation adjacent to the hospital. In order for a hospital to keep graduate nurses, interns and nurses' aides, it is important that they have housing facilities with which to take care of them. Mr. Speaker, I rise to indicate general support for the general principle of this bill, and in particular for those clauses which provide for programs of sewage disposal and dormitories for universities. I am prompted to reply at this time to some remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. The hon. member took great pride in the
National Housing Act
amount of public funds the government is making available for housing. It seems to me this is a very strange position for a member or a party to take which prides itself on its support of private enterprise. The success of our housing program surely does not depend upon the amount of public funds invested in it. The success of any housing program must necessarily depend upon the number of houses built and whether the houses that are built are of a type that meets the needs of the people.
My hon. colleague from Nipissing yesterday, and the hon. member for Welland again today, put on record the fact that in the last three years of the Liberal regime approximately 380,000 houses were built for an expenditure of $65 million of public funds, while the last three years of the present government 415,000 houses have been built for an expenditure of $900 million of public funds. It seems to me that this tremendous increase should be a cause of disquietude. No doubt the government would not invest the money if it did not have to do so, particularly at a time when we are running into heavy deficits. The fact that this money for residential housing is of necessity taken from the public sector raises the question whether free enterprise is really alive to its responsibility to the people of Canada in this regard.
The success of the program depends not only upon the number of houses built, but also upon whether they are the right kind of houses. I was interested in a comment made over the radio this morning by a commentator, I believe it was Mr. Campbell, in which he pointed out that the number of houses being built is far in excess of new family formations. If this is a fact, then one must conclude that the extra houses are being built to replace old houses. I am sure anybody would agree there is a place for public funds in our housing program, but I believe the proper use of public funds is to provide houses for people in the low income brackets, or for those people who will perhaps have to live all their lives in rented accommodation. For them we should be supplying low rental housing.
When the minister replies I should like him to tell us what kind of houses have been built in the last few years with the $900 million that has been spent. Are they expensive houses in the $15,000 to $25,000 bracket, or are they cheaper houses for people with smaller incomes? In my own province we are particularly interested in houses for people in the low income group. I had a special interest in a housing program for fishermen which was announced some time ago but which I believe did not prove to be very successful.

National Housing Act
I do think we should take a good look at where our present housing policy is leading us. It is all right, of course, to provide houses when they are needed, but if our housing program is determined by the necessity to create jobs, then a make work housing program in my view is not compatible with a proper policy for housing. I do hope the minister will give us some indication as to the type of houses which have been built in the main out of the public funds that have so far been expended.
Many hon. members have referred to the high interest rates and the effect these rates have on a person who is taking out a mortgage on a new home. We all hope it will be possible to reduce these interest rates. However, I do not think anybody who looks at the situation realistically can feel that this is going to happen in the very near future, because these high interest rates are a product of our present system. If we are really going to do anything about it we will have to do something about the system that produces these high interest rates. To my mind there is something radically wrong when a person who buys a $15,000 house has to pay $30,000 or $35,000 before he actually owns it. Housing is a necessity, and we should be ingenious enough to work out some system to provide housing for people without imposing upon them this tremendous financial burden.
I ask the minister to see to it that when this new commission that is going to inquire into our financial system is set up they take a good look at this problem and see what changes can be brought about in our whole financial system to correct the present situation.

I should like to say a very few words at this time. We have had several opportunities this session to discuss the subject of housing, so it is not my intention to speak for any undue length of time today. Yesterday I tried to outline the situation as I saw it. As I said at that time, we are in agreement with the principle of the bill.
However, I was very disappointed to notice that government spokesmen were again trying to create the myth that nothing was done in the housing field under Liberal administration, and that a housing utopia has been created under the present administration. I quoted figures again yesterday showing that in the last three years we were in office slightly fewer than 400,000 homes were built.
National Housing Act
In the first three full years of this government's administration, 1958, 1959 and 1960, slightly over 400,000 homes were built. I also pointed out that we were required to put in government funds to the extent of $65 million, while this government for comparable results had to put in $924 million. I observed yesterday that this was a strange example of free enterprise. Spokesmen for this government are always happy to suggest that they are the champions of free enterprise. I know that some hon. gentleman opposite perhaps misunderstood what I said yesterday. I simply wanted to point out that this was indeed a strange example of free enterprise.
I also wish to refer to a statement which was made yesterday by the minister. He tried to get some mileage out of the fact that in the United States this year housing starts are up by only 3 per cent, while in Canada they will be up to a greater degree. We are, of course, all very glad that housing construction will be up in Canada but, as is so often the case, a comparison between Canadian and United States figures is misleading. Housing in the United States had not been depressed in 1960 to the extent that it was depressed here in the same year.
We also regret that there was nothing in the minister's statement which leads us to be encouraged to hope for or expect any early reduction in National Housing Act interest rates. Apparently no government action in this direction is envisaged in the near future. It is known that we on this side have always deplored the increases in costs that are a direct result of high interest rates. This subject was dealt with very ably by my friend the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) and I need not repeat the points he made. I wish to point out, however, that a reduction of 1 per cent in the interest rate on a $12,000 30 year mortgage would mean a saving of approximately $2,300 in the cost of a home. Surely this is deserving of serious attention on the part of this government.
We regret too that the legislation contains nothing that will reduce the high cost of housing. As hon. members know the legislation merely seeks to raise the ceiling on loaning under the existing legislation. It is also a source of regret that there has been no liberalization of the legislation to bring in any new groups of Canadians and particularly those in the lower income bracket who are denied the benefits of this act.
In that vein I should point out that in 1960, 92 per cent of the borrowers under the N.H.A. had an annual income of $4,000 or more. It can be seen that the action taken

National Housing Act
by the government scarcely meets the requirements. Certainly it tails to meet the objectives initially established by the act which was designed to assist Canadians in the lower income groups purchase their own homes. As I said, the present measure deals only with increasing the permissive ceiling.
I close as I began by saying that while we have some reservations about giving the government this much elbow room in what might well be a year preceding an election, we are in agreement with the basic principle of the bill.

In other words, a total of 690 claims have been paid under this insurance fund although, as I have indicated, close to a quarter of a million loans have been made. Therefore, when the hon. member for Welland cries aloud at the havoc being wrought on the poor unfortunate person who has bought our houses, being induced to do so by the blandishments of the Minister of Public Works, may I say that they are not doing too badly when out of that number only 690 claims have been paid.
National Housing Act

If we obey the suggestion of most hon. members of the opposition that we should lower interest rates, what is the situation going to be? I recall it as a nightmare. When I became the minister in August of 1959 the interest rate had been set at 6 per cent and the rate had become unrealistic because the interest rate on bonds had gone up, as my hon. friend knows, with the result that a rate of 6 per cent was unattractive. So far had the interest rates on bonds gone up that even the banks withdrew. They would not lend any money at 6 per cent and loans by private lenders just dribbled out.
One of the things that I am perhaps responsible for was the government offering to take the place of private lenders in 1959 in order to keep housing going and afloat. That is the kind of situation that I dread seeing happen again. I should certainly like to reduce the interest rate and just as soon as I can get advice from the experts which makes it appear to me to be feasible we will reduce the interest rate. We are very anxious to reduce the interest rate. However, with the experience in 1959 involving an unrealistic rate which I have related and with the experience of the Kennedy administration at the present time, which arbitrarily reduced the interest rate by half of 1 per cent with ensuing tragic results, I say to the

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, September 18, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-71 respecting the Civil Service of Canada- Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)-Mr. Chown in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the committee rose last night we were considering clause 7 of the bill and an amendment proposed thereto by the hon. member for Ottawa East.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have promised the parliamentary secretary not to take too much time to express the ideas I might have on this matter.
First of all, I must say that I support wholeheartedly the amendment moved by the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard). I think it would not be too difficult for the government to grant civil servants the right to negotiate, for we have already granted the same right to the employees of certain crown corporations, such as the C.N.R., the C.B.C., and some provinces have even done the same.
The Quebec government, for instance, recently granted, in the case of the Quebec hydro commission, the right to hold direct negotiations between the commission's representatives and those of the employees association. I cannot see why the people who are directly engaged in government service, in the various departments of the federal administration, are treated in a different manner from those who work for crown corporations. Employees in various government departments serve their country and their fellow citizens just like those who are with the commissions and crown corporations, either federal or provincial.
Some people oppose recognition of this right which is fundamental in my opinion for government employees, on the grounds that this would open the door to possible strikes.
It is true that a strike of public service employees or civil servants could cause considerable prejudice to the general public and, in some areas, could even deal a hard blow to the country's economy.

Civil Service Act
However, I do not feel that civil servants want to strike and this is not only my personal opinion, because my statement is based on a brief submitted to the special House of Commons committee by the civil service association of Canada. I would simply like to quote paragraph 69, 21 of that brief:
(Text):
Another dissenting opinion is based largely on the premise that a strike could not be tolerated in the government service. We strongly emphasize that the strike is not now, nor ever has been an issue. Government employees, with some very minor exceptions, do not wish to strike. Rather we prefer impartial arbitration as a method of resolving differences.
(Translation):
I would also like to quote in that regard a paragraph from a study by Mr. S. J. Frankel, entitled: "Arbitration in the British Civil Service", on page 211 which reads as follows:
(Text):
Looking back over 35 years it is clear that arbitration has made a decisive contribution to the development of reasonable and harmonious staff relations. In a society that accepts the full implication of trade unionism it is extremely important that no large body of employees should feel that it is in an inferior position merely because its employer happens to be the state. In a sphere of public activity where the strike would be regarded as disproportionately disruptive, if not intolerable, arbitration seems to offer a fair and reasonable alternative.
(Translation):
There is another objection some people have against the right to negotiate. They say that it would infringe on parliament's authority and supremacy. Here again, the civil service association made a very specific suggestion as shown at page 22 of the brief I mentioned a moment ago, and I should like to read paragraph 73 on the same page, it reads:
(Text):
In the light of the long established and zealously guarded traditions of parliamentary supremacy under the British system, any fears that negotiation and arbitration would in any way invade or lessen parliament's right are completely unfounded. As a safeguard against any possible threat to the supremacy of parliament, the British long ago settled any question of constitutional concern through the acceptance by all concerned of the following formal agreement:
"The establishment of Whitley Councils (i.e. direct negotiation) cannot relieve the government of any part of its responsibility to parliament and ministers, and heads of departments, acting under the general or specific authority of ministers, must take such action as may be required in any case in the public interest. This condition is inherent in the constitutional doctrines of parliamentary government and ministerial responsibility, and ministers can neither waive nor escape it".
(Translation):
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the rights and the authority of parliament and of the

representatives duly elected by the people, are well protected.
As I just said, the United Kingdom found a solution to this problem a long time ago, and I feel that we cannot accuse the mother of parliaments of being unconcerned with the rights of the representatives of the people. New Zealand and Australia have followed its example.
If a disagreement arises between the employer, who is the government, and the employees of the government, this is what happens: in most cases, the employer, having considered the requests made by the employees, establishes himself as judge in the dispute which has arisen between the two parties. While he is the employer, he sets himself up as judge, and I am of the opinion that this situation is completely abnormal.
I believe that the right to direct negotiations should be granted to the association of employees. A conciliation board, independent from the civil service commission, should be set up and, if a conciliation board is not desired, a standing committee of the house could hear the representations following the negotiations, the whole matter being submitted for the approval of parliament, should it be deemed necessary.
It is an honour and a privilege, it is true, to work for one's country. These civil servants of Canada, as many foreigners have stated again and again on various occasions, are second to no other civil service groups in other countries of the world. However, this honour and privilege of dedicating one's life and efforts to the service of one's country should not put the civil servants in an inferior position in relation to their fellow citizens who have taken up employment in private industry.
The government of Canada is one of the largest employers in the country. Hence, it is its duty to set an example for private enterprise not only by maintaining its already cordial relations with its employees, but also by granting them the right to direct negotiations with their employer, and the right of appeal before a conciliation board.
I know that this cannot be accomplished overnight, but I ask the government to reconsider its stand on this problem, so that, at the next session, employees of the federal government can be placed on an equal footing with employees in private enterprise.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, we naturally support the amendment placed before the committee. As is well known the C.C.F. has consistently advocated bargaining rights for employees not only in the public service of

Canada but of the provinces as well. In previous sessions and again this session I have placed on the order paper bills designed to give employees in the public service the right to bargain collectively and to have to a degree a say in the determination of their destiny, in bargaining and in reaching collective agreements with their employers.
It may be that the ideas we proposed are not acceptable in detail and as expressed in previous debates there may exist some disagreement concerning methods and concepts. However, I shall concern myself solely with the principle of the right of employees in the public service to have, as far as possible and practical, the same rights granted to employees in industry and in crown corporations.
We welcome the support latterly given to this concept by the Liberal party. We wish hon. members of that party well in their endeavour and hope that jointly we can convince the government that collective bargaining for employees in the public service should be established.
We should be concerned with equality of treatment among Canadians. I do not think that we can or should differentiate between employees engaged in different types of endeavours. All should have equal rights. A great deal of dissatisfaction develops in the public service of Canada and of various provinces because there is a relatively narrow channel through which those employees can find relief with respect to their particular grievances or to their concepts and ideas of what should be their wages, hours of work and working conditions. I suppose it is possible, and it has been done, to refer to what has occurred in other countries and what has been the experience in another part of Canada with respect to this matter, but I do not know whether that would buttress the argument any more than it has been reinforced at the moment. If we retain the concepts of equality of treatment and attempt to work toward that end we shall be accomplishing far more than we shall accomplish by quoting statistics, figures and systems which may exist in some other parts of the world.
Some years ago the parliament of Canada decided by the enactment of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act that employees working in industry and in crown corporations would have certain rights and freedoms, one of which was the right to band together for their mutual protection within a trade union of their choice. This we think should extend and apply to the employees in the public service of Canada, and it does. There is that right of forming associations, organizations or unions of employees within the public service, and they have the advantage of that.
Civil Service Act
The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act also states that if the employees can show to the labour relations board that a majority of them are members of a particular union, that union is entitled to receive a certificate of bargaining authority. We think this should be the law applicable to the employees in the public service also and there should be equal treatment there.
In industry and in crown corporations the employees have the right, through their bargaining agent, to sit down with their employer and bargain collectively for a collective agreement. We think that in this regard there should be equality of treatment, and there should be freedom of opportunity of individual groups within the public service to do the same thing and have their employer, the crown, sit down and bargain with them.
We think the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act says that an employee shall not be subject to pressures and manipulation by his employer. We think that should be the approach to the problem of the employees in the public service; that they should not be subject to having to go with cap in hand and consult with the Minister of Finance or with anybody else on what should be their just, fair and equitable wages, hours of work and working conditions. We think these things and agreement on them can be reached by the process of open, sincere and honourable collective bargaining between organizations representing employees in the public service and the government itself, or a representative group of the government, just the same as exists in industry and in corporations, and this is the thing that we should like to see.
In so far as strike action is concerned, we feel that this is one field-perhaps it, is the only field-in which there should be a difference of attitude and policy in existence, and that in the public service of Canada there should not be the right to strike. Perhaps this is the attitude of the vast majority of people in the public service of Canada. We think there should not be that right to strike, to use the withdrawal of their ability to work as a final means of obtaining a collective agreement such as exists and takes place from time to time in industry and in crown corporations. We think that in substitution therefor there should be the right of arbitration, the right of employees concerned, through their respective organizations, to present their statistics, their arguments, their reasonings and their briefs to a tribunal and the right on the part of the crown to present arguments, statistics, and so forth on behalf of its proposals and the right of the employees of the public service of

Civil Service Act
Canada to receive a decision by arbitration if necessary as to what should be contained within a collective agreement and what should be their wages, their hours of work and their working conditions.
We think it is unfair and certainly neither in keeping with the spirit which we had when we enacted the bill of rights, nor in keeping with the spirit which is contained within the words of the bill of rights, to have upwards of 130,000 employees in the public service of Canada placed in a category of being in fact second class citizens as compared with the rest of the people of this country.
If this government believes in what it believed when it enacted the bill of rights I think it is time to extend that degree of decency and equality to people in the public service of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question? The question is on the amendment.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add but a few words to what previous speakers have already said about this amendment.
In reading over again the proposed amendment, which is found on page 8023 of Hansard of July 13, 1961, I note that it contains important elements, which are in keeping with the development of rights and freedoms in Canada, particularly in regard to employees.
I have already had the opportunity of taking a stand on that matter, at a civil servants' meeting held in Sherbrooke last year, and I should like to repeat today my attitude towards that problem. I consider that, in the field of rights and freedoms, there has sprung up, as from a valve, a quite natural and logical explosion, a bill of rights, introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), which, actually, has given substance to everyone's needs before the law, and to the prerogatives of all Canadians, regardless of class-but I see in this amendment, as I said, absolutely essential elements which are in keeping with the development of our labour code, and with our social evolution within the present Canadian context.
I have already taken a stand publicly on the matter, in Sherbrooke, and I do so today in the House of Commons, in favour of collective bargaining for civil servants, in order that they may be on the same footing as other workers in private enterprise.
However, I find that in the amendment, as introduced, one reservation is lacking, and that is why I find it incomplete.

Therefore, I should like to point out, as I did in Sherbrooke at that meeting of government employees, that personally-right or wrong?-I am firmly opposed to any kind of strike. Of course, I am in favour of negotiations, I am in favour of arbitration, but I am opposed to the right to strike for government employees, because I want to ensure efficiency in government operations and security for all.
In the last decade, we have but too often heard of groups of government employees calling a strike at some crucial moment, in certain countries, thereby placing their government in a very dangerous position economically and even threatening public security.
That is why I would have liked a more complete amendment whatever the machinery that would make government employees give up the right to strike. Having met over 400 government employees with whom I discussed the matter in the eastern townships, last winter, I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that all were in agreement and energetically demanded the right to negotiate and to arbitration; but they all felt also that the right to strike should be given up.

Mr. Chairman, just a word to reassure the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) who just sat down. He said that he discussed the matter with government employees in his district. I can tell him that we, in the committee, met the spokesmen of all the civil service employees and that they do not want the right to strike. The only group which asked for that right was that of the postmen, whereas, the others were flatly opposed to striking.
I entirely agree with the hon. member for Sherbrooke, and the same situation exists in the province of Quebec, where civil service employees are not given the right to strike. I think civil servants should not be given this right. But, if arbitration is granted, they will never be tempted to call a strike, because we must keep in mind that those employees are in a class different from that of industrial workers, and their problems can always be settled to better advantage by discussions in the House of Commons. I therefore think that they would be satisfied if they did not obtain the right to strike. Indeed, they have no intention of availing themselves of this right, even if it is not prohibited by law.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two. More than once in this

debate the words "second-class citizen" have been used. I want to comment on that for a minute. I point out first of all that civil servants of their own motion have indicated that they do not wish the right to strike. For that I applaud them. Second, may I say that I have had a fair amount to do with civil servants through working with them and I have always enjoyed our association. I have always felt that we were working together in the public interest and that there was something in the quality of their employment which did not exist in any other kind of employment that I knew. While I am not going to say more about the use of the phrase "second-class citizen", I regret its use very much. I feel exactly the opposite about civil servants, and I say with deference that I hope that those who have been using that phrase will abandon it.

I should like to comment with respect to that matter. I am one of those who have used the phrase "second-class citizen". I think the hon. member for Greenwood perhaps misunderstood my application of it. I hope he did. At no time have I considered that employees in the public service are second-class or any other than first-class citizens, together with all other people in this country. What I said was that by virtue of denying these people the opportunities and the rights that exist for other employees, as other clauses in the bill will also indicate, we are in fact treating them as second-class citizens by saying that they do not have equal rights, privileges and responsibilities with other citizens of our country. My use of the phrase was not for the purpose of designating civil servants as second-class citizens but I say that this is in fact what happens when we deny them the rights that other people have. These words have been used on a number of occasions during discussions I have had with employees in the public service who consider they are treated in this way by the government, but I am not applying these words to civil servants as a class of people.
(Translation):

I should like to add a few words to what the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) said earlier to the effect that the group of civil servants which asked for the right to strike was the postal workers group. I take the liberty of pointing out that if the postal workers associations have come to that conclusion, it is because of all civil servants, postal workers are about the worst treated at the present time.
When the Post Office Department's estimates were under consideration, I mentioned a great
Civil Service Act
many reasons why postal workers were complaining, criticizing and asking for better working conditions.
When an association or a group of citizens is desperate, it is not surprising that at one point they should ask for the right to strike. I shall come back to this matter when we discuss the provisions relating to leave.
I should just like to give you an example to illustrate what the situation is. What should we think of the fact that postal employees lost their statutory leave because it fell on a Saturday or a Sunday, or that seasonal and part-time postal employees were compelled to pass examinations even though they were working only two, three or four hours a day?
