speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, December 8, 1960, consideration of the motion of Mr. Peters for the second reading of Bill No. C-7, to provide in Canada for the dissolution and the annulment of marriage.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems as though we were perhaps starting on a new session rather than continuing one which started a year ago as normally bills of this nature-or at least, this has been the experience in latter years-have not too often come up for resumed debate. This matter was entered into quite extensively on December 8 of last year and I think a worth-while and fairly full discussion took place by members who were interested in the principle contained within the bill.

Naturally, as is the case in discussing bills of this nature which emanate from and are in the hands of private members, there was some degree of difference of opinion with respect to some of the provisions contained in the bill. However, I know that the government is in a very amenable and conciliatory mood these days. After this bill receives its second reading we may perhaps be able to straighten out some of these differences of opinion at the committee stage of the bill and then wind up, on third reading in meeting the wishes of the majority of the members of the house.
The design of the bill itself to me is to bring the law-I should not say the statute law because there is none as such-in circumstances relating to divorce in Canada as a whole into conformity with some social facts of life which exist today and which, in my opinion, have existed for some period of time. At the moment the law of divorce, with the exception of that in the province of Nova Scotia, states that the grounds for divorce are adultery and adultery only. In essence that is the situation that exists. However, I think we are all fairly well agreed that while adultery may be the grounds for divorce, it certainly is not, in the great bulk of cases, in the first instance the cause of a marital breakdown and the reason for people seeking to obtain a divorce. There are other factors which go into breaking up a marital relationship. I refer to such things as lack of a full and complete faith, alcoholism, wars, increased travelling facilities and the like. All of these things have their impingement, in my opinion, upon the marital structure and tend perhaps to make marital relationships a bit strained.
However, adultery is the only reason one can use in order to satisfy a court or parliament that a particular marriage should be dissolved. I am certainly not going to get into an argument with anybody as to the percentage or the degree of perjury that takes place before the courts or before parliament. I think this is an argument which does not lead to any end. However, in some cases, or in some instances, the law itself and the requirements of the law either force a person or a couple into an adulterous relationship which did not exist previously, or into perjury or collusion in order to meet the test demanded by the law, namely, that adultery took place between a couple of people.
I think the maintenance of the fiction that adultery is really the cause for divorce is not too sensible in itself. By making that action the sole and only reason or ground upon which a marriage can be dissolved, I think a tendency is created to say that the

marriage relationship rests almost entirely upon the question of intimate relationships between the husband and the wife or, in fact, to say that marriage rests almost exclusively upon the question of amicable sexual intercourse.
We know that is not the case. We know that there are many other factors which go into making up a happy married life and into making and preserving a married relationship and the marriage itself. I think many of these other factors are forgotten in the desire to maintain adultery, as is the situation at the moment, as the only ground and, by reasoning the only cause for divorce.
As it stands now, the law does not take into account, give any relief to, or open the door to those people who find themselves in some circumstances which I intend to relate in a moment or two. For these people who, through no fault of their own in many cases, find themselves in difficulties there is no solution having regard to their marital relationships.
Let us consider an instance of desertion in which, for argument's sake, let us say the husband deserts his wife and family, if there is one. If that husband cannot be found, as is the case in many instances of which I know, the wife is maintained in that position of being married yet single at the same time She has no recourse to the courts in order to have dissolution of that marriage, even though her husband may have vanished and his whereabouts have been unknown to her for many years, and even though she is unable to find him.
I think each of us desires the company of others. In many instances women and men will find themselves attracted to some other person of the opposite sex. They are then placed on the horns of a dilemma. They ask themselves the question: What should my relationship be with this other person? Should it be one of just casual acquaintance or should we become more closely associated with each other? They say to themselves: If we do so, we shall have to do so without the benefit of a marriage being performed as one of us is already married and is unable to obtain any relief. There is no relief either in instances of extreme cruelty, alcoholism coupled with cruelty, or dissipation on the part of the husband of income which should be used for the upkeep and the welfare of his wife and family. There is no relief in sight for that particular woman except perhaps that of suing in the court for maintenance; and in many instances this procedure does not work out too satisfactorily. Others with habitual criminal tendencies and the like bring to mind other instances of one part or one half of the marriage being unable
90205-6-540
Private Bills
to find any relief whatsoever in the eyes of the law in so far as trying to straighten out their marital relationships is concerned.
Some people might say that this bill, if it were enacted, would in fact tend to make divorce easier and therefore tend to corrupt our present morals and tend to destroy as an institution marriage itself. However, I do not think this is the case. I think, as I said, all this bill is designed to do is bring our present divorce laws into keeping with social facts and what I think should be social conscience in this day and age.
I would refer to the statitistical information which developed in England after the passage of their matrimonial causes act. Reference to this statistical information is not to say that the same thing would apply here, of course, However, if I recall correctly from memory, I think they discovered that after the grounds for divorce were brought into keeping with the social facts which existed at the time, it did not in fact destroy the marriage system. It may have dissolved particular marriages by giving grounds for the dissolution of marriage, but if I recall the figures correctly, over a period of time 75 per cent or 80 per cent of those who were divorced at one time subsequently married again and stayed that way. This tends to show that while a marriage may be dissolved, it does not mean that the parties concerned stay single for the rest of their lives but they do find other partners and the marriage contract is entered into again with somebody else.
The bill does not primarily deal with divorce itself, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and other hon. members. It places a certain degree of emphasis upon the question of reconciliation and gives to the judge hearing a particular case the right to adjourn, to refer the parties to marriage counsellors, to clergymen or other people of similar standing, in the hope that divorce action can be forestalled and that the marriage will remain intact. In this way it is hoped to find some mutuality of desire on the part of the parties to continue in their original way in their married life without dissolving the marriage.
I do not intend to enter into the relative grounds of this argument, but it has been mentioned and I am sure we all feel there is a degree of hypocrisy which arises out of our present divorce laws. There is a certain degree of dishonesty and perjury. I am quite sure this is well known to members-at least some-of the legal profession. I am sure it is quite well known and understood to exist in so far as the courts are concerned. This is in no way casting reflections on the courts or

Private Bills
members of the legal profession. It is well known by private detectives and I am sure we as legislators have knowledge of it. It does exist to a certain extent. It is also known to the general public, certainly to those who have become involved in divorce actions in a direct way as one of the litigants.
This bill, of course, would not eliminate perjury, collusion or dishonesty in the presentation of cases before the courts. It is not designed to do that. However, I think it would tend to cut it down because it would recognize desertion, cruelty and the like as other grounds for divorce.
Again, if I recall correctly some statistics emanating from Great Britain after the passage of the matrimonial causes act in that country, all but about 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the divorces were granted for either adultery, desertion or cruelty. These are perhaps the three major complaints and grievances that exist at the present time in society. As I say, this bill would not eliminate that; it would only tend to cut it down and bring the law itself more in keeping and on a more equitable footing with what in fact exists in society today.
I was being a little facetious earlier, Mr. Speaker, when I said we could straighten out some of these difficulties in committee of the whole, because I do not think we are going to get that far. I do not think this bill will receive passage this session. I do not think it will come to a vote, although I should certainly like to see it come to a vote. But with our forces disseminated the way they are, we would not even be able to call a vote if we got that far. I can say that at least in this one instance our party is unanimous today.
However, some day I am quite sure that a bill containing the principles contained in the present bill will be passed and endorsed by a parliament of Canada and will be introduced by a government of Canada. We all know that to some degree bills and legislation tend to lag behind public need and public demand. This is not always the case, but it is the case in some instances. Legislation tends to lag behind public demand when it is of such great importance as to create major differences of opinion based on fundamental beliefs and ideals.
That is the case in this instance. I think in this connection we must respect the feelings and desires of everyone in the country and we must come to the conclusion that it will be some time yet before the parliament of Canada does get around to passing a measure such as this. But some day it will occur and I think that when the statute law of Canada reflects the social matters, principles and ideas contained within this particular bill

it will be appropriate to pay a very great tribute to the hon. member for Timiskaming who drafted, developed and primarily conceived the ideas and concepts contained in this bill. We should pay a tribute to the hon. member at that time for having the courage to bring forward such a far-reaching measure as this bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
First of all I wish to approve of the last sentence expressed by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I think it would be most reprehensible, having in mind the fact that these people have come to the ultimate seat of justice in this country seeking what they feel is an appropriate remedy, if they were denied that remedy at a time when they may have no other recourse. I do hope that before we conclude our deliberations in this chamber this will be done.
I also wish to associate myself with what the hon. member said with regard to those who participated in this debate on December 8. This was one of the debates which, I think, brought out a very high quality of contribution from the members who spoke. I think there has been great diligence shown in doing research work. I think there was sincerity and honesty displayed by all those who spoke at that time and I think that, like the debate having to do with capital punishment, without in any way disparaging other debates, it was an indication of the heights to which hon. members can rise when there is a deep social problem involved and corrective measures may well be required. As to that, I think there is no doubt.
I can recall many years ago in a northern town included in the district where I practised my profession one week when I participated in three murder trials each of which involved a husband and wife. In each of these cases the situation might well have been cured by the ability to obtain a dissolution of the marriage. I think it is a drastic way to have to get a divorce, to use a shotgun, but this was my experience many years ago and I have never forgotten it. I recall that after the war when I resumed my practice I was shocked by the large number of 90205-6-540J
Private Bills
applications from people seeking dissolution of their marriages. I think it was probably the experience of many members of the bench and of the bar, that these were the result of too hasty marriages. But it does underline the fact that there is a very real and serious problem. Those who read history can establish that when you see the disintegration of our family life you may then see the deterioration of the civilization in which it was produced.
There is a very interesting series of articles appearing in Life magazine-and I think we can take wide latitude in dealing with this particular subject matter. I happened to pick up this magazine last night and I commend the reading of this article to all members. It deals with the entire question of marriage and divorce. Contributions come from trained sociologists and people who have had a great deal of experience in conncetion with this problem. The article I picked up deals with what is probably one of the reasons for the multiplicity of divorces. I think that what the hon. member is trying to strike at in his bill is rather the effect than the cause, but this particular article deals with the question of courtship, which is related to marriage, and I am going to take the liberty of reading a few extracts. This is from Life magazine dated September 15, 1961, and I am reading from page 118. The article says:
Because there were no sociologists until recently to study and record such matters, the history of courtship is obscure. There is every reason to presume, however, that very few civilized people of bygone eras ever had as much freedom of choice as today's young Americans. To be sure, the people who did not count, like the serfs of the Middle Ages, having no property, no prospects and no real control over their own futures, mated casually and often without benefit of clergy. But the lords in the feudal castles were much more careful-for ever since men first began accumulating property, rank, social prestige and pride of lineage, they have tried to preserve and augment these acquisitions through marriage. The rulers of ancient Rome would never have thought of letting a daughter marry a commoner. The Capulets did not even want their Juliet to fool around with the Montagues' Romeo.
And again, with respect to arranged marriage:
Thanks to a thousand overromantic novels, plays and movies, it is commonly thought of as an attempt to force a lovely and innocent young girl into the arms of some disgusting old lecher who has slipped her greedy father a couple of thousand dollar bills-a situation calculated to make any good American's blood boil... Yet in weeping for all the poor girls forced into marriage against their will in other countries, Americans may have been wasting their sympathy. Dr. David Mace, executive director of the American Association of Marriage Counselors, says in his "Marriage East and West" that many of these downtrodden victims of the arranged marriage have not seemed to mind at all. Indeed, young women from the Far East, observing western courtship customs for the

Private Bills
first time, have often wound up feeling sorry for the American girls who have been feeling so sorry for them. The idea of being forced to go out alone into the open market, and to preen and flirt in the hope of attracting a husband, strikes many Oriental women as terribly undignified and demeaning.
I hasten to add that I am not adopting this particular philosophy. I just offer it to the house as an indication of the problem that is now being considered carefully by many thoughtful people.
I say to the hon. member for Skeena and to the sponsor of this bill that I have grave doubts as to whether the legislation which they propose will do anything other than regularize divorce by opening up more avenues for divorce, a situation which they cannot ever hope to cure.
This bill is difficult to deal with on second reading because I believe it involves a variety of subject matters. There are a number of principles on related matters all brought together within the four corners of the bill. Under those conditions I assume I might be granted some latitude in dealing with the principles of the individual proposals which are incorporated in the proposed measure.
In the first instance it seems to me there is a real jurisdictional question which is thrown out by the principles contained in this bill. The argument was developed in this debate when the bill was first before us for consideration, that the British North America Act divided between the provincial legislatures and the federal government certain aspects of marriage and divorce. Item 26 of section 91 of the British North America Act gives to the federal government jurisdiction over the question of marriage and divorce. Section 92, on the other hand, gives to the provincial legislatures the power to deal with the solemnization of marriage in the province. I have had no opportunity to examine the records and debates at the time the fathers of confederation enacted their agreement and the reason for this division is obscure to me. I do not think any real arguments can be made about it.
I suggest that this government has been diligent under the leadership of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) in securing certain reforms in connection with the constitution, including the repatriation of the British North America Act and including consideration of the question of the delegation of powers and of certain other changes in our constitution. This might well be a subject which could be placed on the agenda at a federal-provincial conference.
When he participated in this debate on a previous occasion the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) gave what I think was his legal opinion when

he said that so far as the province of Quebec is concerned the entire jurisdiction might well fall squarely in the lap of that province. I think the hon. gentleman went a little far in making that statement but the questions of marriage, divorce and the solemnization of marriage do appear to be related. It may be that the people in certain areas, districts and provinces, hold certain views about these problems. If a conference were held at which these questions could be discussed freely and openly the conclusion might be reached that the matter is one which could be dealt with by a change in the British North America Act which would have the effect of giving back to the provinces the entire jurisdiction in this field. I do not say I adopt that view but it is something that might well be considered.
The problems concerning jurisdiction are in my opinion underlined when we come to read the bill. We find so many areas where there is likely to be a multiplicity of litigation. If the bill were to be adopted as it stands I can readily see that the courts of this country would be flooded with litigation. Some of it would go to appeal and in many instances two or three years would require to elapse before there could be a final determination by the ultimate court, the Supreme Court of Canada. I throw out that suggestion for consideration by the house.
For example, I shall deal with one of the principles involved in the portion of this bill relating to the question of domicile which creates a genuine problem. The sponsor of this bill suggests that there should be a Canadian domicile. That might be all right but a practical problem would necessarily follow. In the case of a couple living in Ontario, the husband might seek his recourse in the courts of the province of British Columbia. Under such circumstances, what would happen if the parties continued to live in Ontario? What about the question of enforcement of the order of the court? What about the questions of alimony, support for and, maintenance of the children and custody of the children? A definite problem would arise of which we cannot rid ourselves simply by saying we will establish a Canadian domicile in divorce to make it possible for those seeking dissolution to go to the courts of any province. I believe that would create many more problems than it would solve.
Clause 6 of the bill sets out a large numbei of grounds which would enable a court to dissolve a marriage. Some of those listed are already grounds for dissolution. Contrary to what was said by the hon. member for Skeena, unnatural conduct and bestiality are at present grounds upon which the courts will grant divorce. Did I hear the hon. member object

to that statement? Possibly I did not. In any event I can assure the hon. member that that is the case and that the courts have on many occasions granted dissolution of marriage on such grounds.
In the case where a party had been guilty of gross cruelty in the first month after marriage, I think it would be monstrous to suggest that it should be tolerated for longer than a month and it should not be necessary to demand that the marriage persist for a further period of one year before dissolution is granted. I think that is wrong and improper. Some of the other grounds set out in clause 6 might be deserving of consideration but I certainly could not lend my support to legislation which opens up, as this bill seems to, so many avenues for dissolution of the sacred contract of marriage on such flimsy grounds.
We come now to the question of procedural matters under the B.N.A. Act. The provincial legislatures have authority in connection with the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts including the procedure in civil matters in those courts. In reading the bill we find that a conflict arises immediately. This measure suggests there should be attached to the courts a conciliation process and it goes far in outlining in detail precisely how the court should operate, how the judges should act, what procedure should be adopted and so on. At first blush I should be inclined to think that this is an infringement of the powers of the provincial legislatures to deal with the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts.
On the question of evidence, recently several legislatures in western Canada have amended their evidence acts so as to permit certain types of evidence to be given in divorce cases which, under the Russell case in England, had not been permissible before. Clause 11 of this bill which we are considering makes certain evidence permissible. I would have grave doubts whether this clause is not ultra vires, having in mind authority given to the provincial governments.
There are many other aspects of this bill that I could deal with and possibly if at some time the bill gets into committee those matters can be considered in detail.
Before I conclude with this particular aspect of the matter I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters). They have made themselves masters of this subject. I would think that since after the next election it is most likely they may be seeking other employment they may well put to good use the knowledge they have acquired and might collaborate in writing a book which could well be
Private Bills
known among the members of the legal profession as "Peters and Howard on Parliamentary Divorce". I would look forward to the publication of such a book.
Speaking seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think there is a problem here. I do commend those who have participated in the debate. I think this is something with which we will have to come to grips. Anyone who examines statistics with regard to this question of the break-up and dissolution of marriages must feel that remedies must be sought, but I think we will have to go farther than simply attempting to deal with the results, and we might better turn our attention to some of the causes.

subtopic: MEASURE TO MODERNIZE DISSOLUTION AND ANNULMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject before us today, involving as it does the question of statistics of married couples and how the problem of divorce can be resolved, is one on which I should like to speak with extreme diffidence. In my opinion there is nothing that can so arouse the enmity of the ordinary man in the street, so arouse the emotions of such a broad range of people as to consider lightly the processes by which or the reasons for which that state of matrimony may be dissolved. For instance, I should like to quote from page 614 of Hansard, where the remarks of the hon. member who introduced the bill may be found. In the lefthand column we find the following:
We have received hundreds of letters, and very few of them have been opposed to broadening the grounds upon which divorce is granted. While I would not go so far as to suggest that, in a political sense, this would be dishonest, I do suggest that it might not be politically sound. Surely a member of parliament does not have to listen to every crackpot in his particular riding.
I am sure that on reflection the hon. member will not say that everyone who disagrees with his bill, certainly with the manner in which it is presented, is a crackpot. On reading this over I sometimes wonder whether the hon. member believes that those who are opposed to broadening the grounds for divorce must themselves be crackpots. Certainly the manner in which the bill is presented, the wholesale recommendations contained therein and the extent to which the grounds for divorce have been broadened lead me to believe that the hon. gentleman who introduced the bill is at least most impatient of the views of those he believes hold marriage to be much too sacred. As we know, there are probably represented in this house various opinions on how sacred are the bonds of matrimony and to what extent they may be loosened by any action of this house in easing the manner of getting rid of them.

Private Bills
The hon. member who just preceded me touched on a very valid point when he suggested that perhaps we should be giving greater thought to the grounds of divorce. There was also his point on the ease of entering into the bonds of matrimony. An examination of the laws of various European countries will show that in most instances certainly getting married is not the simple task it is here. In certain countries it involves very definite compliance with the canons of church law and long drawn out legal procedures. It usually ties in the question of property settlement and the ways in which the wife shall share in her property. All this, Mr. Speaker, is merely an illustration of the fact that matrimony is a subject that cannot be taken lightly. The fact that it has perhaps been entered into too lightly in this country leads to the rather more furious search for the means of getting rid of it.
The hon. member who introduced this bill made another remark in his speech that I could not quite agree with. At the top of page 613, in the left hand column, he said:
We have felt that the House of Commons cannot rule efficiently on divorce petitions, and are concerned about cases of this type and their effect on the work of the house and the other place as well. It seems to me that members of parliament and members of the other place, many of whom were formerly members of parliament or are public spirited citizens, do not have the ability to judge these cases and in most cases they do not have the inclination to act as a judicial body.
I think it would be most unkind to consider passing the bill before us today on the ground that members of the other house do not have the ability or the inclination to deal adequately with the problems presented to them. It is my opinion that most of the members of the Senate committee dealing with divorce are retired or still practising members of the bar. Before they came to that Senate committee most of them had had many years of experience in divorce matters. Certainly, over the last few years, considering the number of divorces that have been handled by that house, any member of fairly long standing on that committee is likely to be one of the most qualified by way of experience in Canada for dealing with divorce. I submit therefore that to suggest they are not qualified is to overlook the facts completely. If we are to take away from the Senate the duty and obligation of looking into and in effect trying these cases, certainly we should not let it be said that we did it on that most unkind ground that they are not capable.
The fact of the experience of the tribunal trying cases of divorce has been brought home to me very forcibly. I believe that if we examine closely the cases tried by the Senate

we will not find there any lack of attention to them, any lack of willingness to examine the evidence carefully and closely. What appears to us sometimes to be very hurried dealing with these matters is not actually the case, I suggest, because with their experience, their knowledge of human nature and the number of cases they have handled they are able to see in a much better perspective and much more quickly exactly what is at the heart of any particular case presented to them.
As a lawyer I have handled many divorce cases and I have listened to many being presented. I have learned that experience and an older and wiser head can sometimes save a lot of time or point out some place where either I or the lawyer handling the case has missed a point. I recall having heard a case presented in the supreme court in Edmonton and the judge on the bench ordering that a copy of the transcript be sent to the Queen's proctor. This meant, of course, that the attorney general's department would be asked to look into the matter, to investigate the validity of the evidence given and to find out if perjury had been committed quite apart from the alleged adultery. I was amazed that the judge should so order in that case because to me it had seemed to fit the pattern. In my opinion the witnesses had appeared very honest and yet the judge, with far more years of experience, had detected a false note and had the matter investigated.
It turned out that a charge of perjury was laid and also one of suborning perjury not because adultery had not been committed but because the defendant's husband-this is where human nature and the peculiarities of personality come into the picture-who had been willing to give his wife evidence of his adultery apparently decided that he did not have the nerve to stand up in court and persuaded a friend of his to get up and say that he had been present on this particular evening and had witnessed just enough to satisfy the court. Investigation by the police proved that the friend had not been there at all that evening although it did come out that the act complained of which constituted grounds for the divorce had in fact been committed. Only the peculiarity of the personality of one man caused this divorce to go astray in the courts. I have cited this case merely as an illustration of the manner in which the experience of the tribunal can play such an important part and of how the manner and demeanor of the witnesses and the circumstances related can so often lead the court to discern the true from the spurious testimony.
As to the question of the grounds for divorce, I have had, as I am sure most hon.

Civil Service Act AFTER RECESS
members have, requests from people to do something about the grounds for divorce. Certainly I am not one of those who are convinced that no matter what happens a divorce should not be granted. I think it is necessary, and in fact on humanitarian grounds I feel that our present divorce law must be broadened a little. It does not hurt to remind hon. members of the extreme hardship that befalls a woman who has entered into the bonds of matrimony with as much care and forethought as anyone in the community and who has in fact chosen a very good husband when later the man suffers some slight injury which affects his mind and he becomes incurably insane. Certainly it is hard for this or any other body to say that it is right that this woman who has suffered this misfortune must stay married forever to this man.
I can well understand the argument of those who say that you marry for better or for worse, that medical science, good as it is, is still not an exact science, that there is no such thing as a hopeless case and that this is an instance where the woman should have a little more faith and patience. It is a little hard to follow that argument too far if the woman has children to raise. Certainly under today's conditions it is hard enough for a husband and wife both of whom are working to raise, feed, clothe and educate a couple of children. For a woman who is still married to try to run a house and earn a livelihood for her children and to be faced with such a situation with no hope of relief until the children grow up is, I think, being so strict that we should yield to the argument that this at least we must correct.
In my opinion there are many causes for divorce listed in clause 6 of the bill for which strong arguments can also be advanced, but I was struck by one thing. The causes for divorce set out in the bill include nearly all the causes for judicial separation that now exist. I do not know whether it is a case of experience, good planning or just good luck, but if there is one thing which I wholeheartedly support it is that I would much rather see a divorce than a separation. If these grounds are good enough to break up a marriage by means of a separation, they should be sufficient grounds for a divorce. I think that the most unsatisfactory method that we have in this country today for dealing with irreparable differences between husband and wife is to give them a judicial separation. They are neither married nor single and in nearly all cases the financial results are most regrettable.

But, in my opinion, even with the best intentions on the part of the commission, injustice could prevail and go on for some time before it was even detected or suspected. On that account I can well understand the hon. member for Hull suggesting some amendment to the clause.
The wording of the suggested amendments is somewhat clumsy. I am not sure that they are put in the best form or that the best

Civil Service Act
phraseology is used to achieve the end the hon. member for Hull has in mind. I must say I think this is rather an overriding clause and makes it possible for injustice to be done without being detected possibly for some time.
People are human, deputy ministers as well as anyone else. Therefore, while I am not certain that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hull is the best type of amendment to meet the situation, because I believe in its spirit and purpose I intend to support it on that account.

Before the question is put I would point out to the committee of the whole that clause 39 reads:
The commission may authorize a deputy head to exercise and perform any of the powers or functions of the commission under this act in relation to the selection of candidates for a position.
The language used is the widest language that can be used in describing the powers or functions of the commission in relation to the selection of candidates for a position. Whatever may be said about the amendment, it is certain that the clause as it stands is expressed in overwide language.

On clause 40-Order of preferences. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I think that over the years there has been, unintentionally perhaps, discrimination against those who joined the forces to fight overseas but who, for some reason or other, and often because of the requirements of the Department of National Defence, were never able to get there.
Those people, who enlisted with the intention to get into the fighting line, but who remained in Canada-and I know several of them-because of their special abilities and because they were needed here, now are absolutely deprived of all special benefits granted to veterans.
I appreciate that those who went overseas should benefit from the terms of this legislation as they did under the old act, which is identical, but I think we should add some special provision with regard to those who did not get overseas, giving them some privilege over other candidates who were not in the services.
To this end, I thought of an amendment which would probably give us a chance to do justice to those who enlisted to fight overseas

but who were detained in Canada against their will and their intent because their services were required here.
I move therefore, that clause 40 be amended to read as follows: After paragraph (b), add subparagraph (i) as it exists now, and which reads:
(b) those who are veterans and who do not come within the provisions of paragraph (a), or who are widows of veterans, shall be placed, in order of merit, on the list immediately following the candidates, if any, mentioned in paragraph (a);
That subparagraph (i) be added, which is the very provision we are dealing with:
Those who are veterans but who have served only in Canada shall benefit from an additional 5 per cent on the examination and shall be placed in order of merit.
(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this deals with a very difficult and very sensitive problem. As one who is not a veteran I have some trepidation in dealing with it, but I have had many problems with respect to this particular situation. The submission I would make to the committee of the whole is this. In respect of these matters the house has generally taken the opinions and the views of the standing committee on veterans affairs. On different occasions that standing committee has made a study of this question and it has been the view of that committee that the provisions of the existing Civil Service Act should remain. I believe it is because of the respect which the special committee on the Civil Service Act had for the standing committee on veterans affairs that the special committee adopted the same attitude.
When this matter was examined by the government, and it was examined with very great care, the position taken, according to my understanding, was that there should be no change in the existing act until such a change had been recommended by the standing committee on veterans affairs. I believe that is a sound position for the house to take. If there is to be a change at any time in such covenants as have been entered into by parliament with the veterans who served overseas, I would hope that they would be made upon recommendation of the standing committee on veterans affairs.

Is there any reason why veterans in receipt of a pension-I presume it means a disability pension-include only those who have served in world war I or world war II? It seems to me that this provision is going to become progressively out of date. Surely we have veterans from the Korean expedition, perhaps some from Egypt and possibly some from Africa, and maybe there will be others. Is there any rational

explanation of this special exception? I am not questioning it; I am simply asking for information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that perhaps complexity of draughtsmanship may be the cause of my hon. friend's difficulty in relation to this matter. The situation is covered, I think, by subclause 3 of clause 40 where there is reference to the Veterans Benefit Act. Under the Veterans Benefit Act veterans of the Korean war are covered and therefore are brought within the ambit of this provision. As lawyers my hon. friend and I may think that is complex draughtsmanship but because of the fact that this particular section has stood for so many years it was the view of the draughtsman, I believe, that it should not be changed fundamentally.

Mr. Chairman, I want to comment on the point of view of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. The amendment I have moved does not affect at all the status of veterans who served overseas. It simply gives a slight advantage in the case of those who enlisted with the intention of going overseas but never had the chance to go. The amendment will not affect other veterans at all. It just gives an additional 5 per cent after the examination has been passed to those who remained in Canada, but those who were overseas have the usual green light. They have the preference over everyone else. The amendment does not change the law in that regard. I do not see why the government cannot accept the idea that a little something should be given to those who intended to go overseas but could not do so because the Department of National Defence ordered them to remain in Canada for the duration of the war. I do not understand why this amendment cannot be accepted when it does not change in any way the status of those veterans who served overseas.

I should like to say a word about what the hon. member for Carleton has said. He has been reminding the committee that the special committee has dealt carefully with these things. I should like to add that, having been here for a good many years I know the veterans affairs committee has dealt year after year with the rights and privileges of veterans. In my opinion no committee has taken its duties so seriously and has been so anxious to be sure to do not only what was fair but perhaps more than fair to those concerned. For that reason I am content to vote against the amendment.

Is there not a danger that the veterans affairs committee might have forgotten those who enlisted to serve throughout the world but were kept in Canada? They could have forgotten about them because
Civil Service Act
generally speaking when we refer to veterans we have in mind those who served overseas. The others were in the services but we do not think of them in that way. The amendment simply affords a little recognition of the services they rendered by enlisting to go and serve throughout the world. If they pass their examination they may get 90 per cent and the amendment would give them an additional 5 per cent and the chance to be first on the list. It will not affect in any way those who served overseas or the status of anyone else. The purpose is simply to recognize the service of those who enlisted to serve overseas but were kept in Canada against their will, and there are many of them.

On clause 47-Language.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, this is a most interesting question and a very significant one. Delegations have come to the committee to speak about the advantages of bilingualism. Nobody can deny that those advantages are infinitely important in the federal government service.
I do not think that anything has been proposed which would be likely to promote the study of both official languages of this country. The civil service should try to offer some special encouragement in order to incite those who are now in the civil service and want to be promoted, and even those who

Civil Service Act
want to enter the civil service, to make an effort to improve their knowledge of both languages.
I know that the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) suggested that the civil service set up some courses to enable those who are now working in the civil service, and those who want to enter that service, to prepare themselves by a better training in respect of bilingualism.
I shall not go as far as to ask for an absolute preference for bilingual people, though I believe that we should in all fairness, do so, because we need them more than we think.
Of course, in some cases, bilingual employees are asked for, but in others, they are forgotten. I remember that, not very long ago, a superintendent for the post office in Ottawa was not required to be bilingual, though he was responsible for the post offices in the ridings of Pontiac, Gatineau, Hull, Papineau, part of Labelle, Argenteuil, and part of eastern Ontario. Yet, the great majority of the population in those districts is French Canadian.
The needs of bilingualism were disregarded. I am not blaming this government more than any other. This situation has obtained for a long time. But it is high time to correct it.
That is why, in order to have some incitement, I move the following amendment to clause 47. Clause 47 will become section 1 and the following section 2 will be added. It reads as follows:
47. (2) At the time of competition those candidates who can establish that they possess a sufficient knowledge of the two official languages of Canada shall benefit by an added 5 per cent over all other candidates and shall be placed in order of merit.
(Text):
In English the amendment reads as follows:
That clause 47 in the bill become subclause (1) and that the following be added as subclause 2:
47 (2) At the time of competitions, those candidates who can establish that they possess a sufficient knowledge of the two official languages of Canada shall benefit by an added five per cent over all other candidates and shall be placed in order of merit.
(Translation) :

Mr. Chairman, I am inclined to share the views of my friend from Hull about section 47 of the present act.
Past experience has shown that a statute can lend itself to various interpretations. Therefore, if the wording is so flexible as to leave it to a high official to judge the degree of bilingualism of an employee, I think that some categories of employees run the risk of being forgotten or overlooked in favour of

others-they are very few, but they might be important-who may be prejudiced against a certain group of citizens.
I must say that the present government has made serious efforts to improve the knowledge of the French language in the civil service.
However, as far as the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hull is concerned, I wonder if the proposed formula is accurate enough for preference to be limited to the candidate who has obtained 5 per cent more marks because he speaks French and English. In my opinion, the knowledge of one of the official languages of the country should represent a higher percentage of the marks.
In my opinion, the government would do well to rewrite this clause so as to give it more teeth, so as to make it more accurate. It should definitely and absolutely provide that preference be given to candidates who are truly bilingual.
As for the degree to which a person is bilingual, that could be the subject matter of another amendment which would recognize the value of bilingualism. The civil service commission could be entrusted with the task of establishing a certain scale.
As far as I am concerned, I approve the principle of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hull, and I commend my hon. friend for his idealism.
(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No clause of the act has had more careful and detailed consideration than has this one. It is a difficult and sensitive one. The language of the draftsman has been most carefully chosen in order to try to achieve an objective which will be sensitive to national unity. I should like to point out to the committee that in the first instance the old act, in section 17, required the language only of the majority of the persons in the local office with whom that person was required to do business. In other words we start from the premise that the existing situation is the local office. The new act deals not only with the local office but with the department. In that sense it is a departure from what has been the precedent in the old act.
I wish to submit to the committee that there are two extremely important tests and that these tests have been expressed in carefully chosen language. The first test is:
-sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately-
The second test is this:
-to give effective service to the public.

As I have said, that is language which was most carefully considered and which was designed to meet what is unquestionably a most difficult problem. My submission to the committee is that this is a problem for administrative as opposed to legislative action; that in legislative action it might well be that you create a strait jacket which will not achieve the purpose the hon. member for Hull professes to have in mind. If the purpose can be achieved within the limits of these two tests by administrative procedure, that is something which I am sure would meet the wishes of all hon. gentlemen of the committee. Therefore my suggestion is that those two tests are sufficient and, because of the careful consideration given to this matter, ought to be adopted by the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word or two in support of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hull. I think it is a good amendment; I think it is very sound.
Throughout this country we have a great and growing need for people, not only in the civil service but elsewhere, to be able to speak the two languages. I think anything to encourage this, such as is suggested in the amendment, is very worth while. I see no reason why this should be a drawback in any way, shape or form and I can think of many, many cases in which this would be a decided asset. I think it is a very sound amendment and I support it fully.

Mr. Chairman, I followed very closely the remarks made by the hon. member for Carleton. The amendment which is now proposed does not in any way change what is the law. I think what we have before us at the moment is better than we had before, but it is not quite enough yet because it does not give the incentive to those who would be interested in learning the two languages. The additional 5 per cent on their remuneration would encourage people to learn the secondary language and would not change the bill as it is now.
It would be an incentive to those who may be interested in learning the secondary language if they could earn more by reason of so doing. I do not blame a person who does not need it and who does not learn the secondary language, but if people have an incentive to earn something out of it, they will do so. This is the reason for placing this amendment before the committee. (Translation):
And I would agree with the hon. member who had the floor a moment ago that what I propose is not momentous, it is but a speck
Civil Service Act
of dust in the universe. But I am convinced that we must not effect changes overnight. We should start from this speck of dust and quietly eliminate that laziness of the mind from which we all suffer, once the necessity of two languages or the intellectual superiority gained through the knowledge of two languages is understood. We learn a second language when we feel the need for it. Such an attitude would encourage civil servants to study a second language more assiduously since this would give them a chance for promotion in the civil service. This is why I moved this amendment.

Civil Service Act
the question why something so curiously vague should be in the bill at all?

On clause 50-Tenure of office. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, clause 50 introduces something which is extremely peculiar. Section 50(1) reads as follows:
The tenure of office of an employee is during the pleasure of Her Majesty, subject to the provisions of this and any other act and the regulations thereunder, and, unless some other period of employment is specified, for an indeterminate period.
Now the peculiar point is in subclause (2):
Nothing in this act shall be construed to limit or affect the right or power of the governor in council to remove or dismiss any employee.
I feel that the government here is assuming powers that are slightly too discretionary. It seems to reserve to ministers or to the governor in council the power to ignore everything else in the act and, at their own discretion to dismiss whoever might be recommended to them for dismissal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I shall have only
two or three statements to make in connection with this amendment. This particular subclause is merely a preservation of the over-all prerogative of the crown. It is in the existing act and it was never repealed-[DOT] a provision that nothing should impair the power of the governor in council to remove any deputy head, officer, person or employee. This subclause merely carries on that provision.
I think it is significant that the maintenance in this bill of this particular subclause which the hon. member seeks to delete was approved by all three members of the civil service commission who appeared before the special committee as witnesses. It is also significant that no representations of any kind were made in relation to it by any of the civil service staff associations. I think the hon. member is well aware of how carefully in clause 60 new provisions have been set forth dealing with dismissals and the right of appeal. This particular provision merely preserves the over-all prerogative of the crown, one which I am sure will not at any time be abused. In view of this I shall ask the committee to reject the amendment.

The subclause as it now stands reads:
2. Nothing in this act shall be construed to limit or affect the right or power of the governor in council to remove or dismiss any employee.

This appears on first reading to be very wide in its language and undoubtedly it is, but I do not see any way of restricting that right-one which I hope will never be abused, though in accordance with the language as it appears in the bill it certainly could be abused. But I do not see any satisfactory way of restricting that right. It seems to me that a government has to be held responsible for the administration and the discharge of its duties and that in line with that responsibility there must be this power of dismissal.
I recall a situation which developed in this country some 15 years ago in which this power was of real value to a government. I am not aware of the provision ever having been abused. It seemed to me as I listened to my colleague moving his amendment that the circumstances in which this provision might be required were not fully understood, and I wonder if he would not consider withdrawing the amendment. I am not altogether happy with the language as it now stands, but I have nothing better to suggest.

I have now heard something about the reason why the provision was placed in this bill, and I think I can accept the suggestion of my colleagues not to present this amendment if that is the wish of the committee.
