speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no criticism of the objective which my hon. friend has in mind. Certainly I think every person who may be dismissed ought to know of his right of appeal. But I have not the slightest doubt that they will in fact know of it. This problem was carefully considered by the special committee. The reason the special committee did not adopt the suggestion, as I recall it, was that it would be necessary for the draughtsman to go through the act completely and in every case where reference was made to a right of appeal insert in the section an indication that notification must be given the employee. Otherwise, by principles of interpretation, where this was not in fact inserted in the section there would be grave difficulties.
If my hon. friend were to press this point the only thing that could happen would be that the clauses would be held up and would require to be referred back to the draughtsmen. I do not think this is a practical problem, quite frankly. I say to the committee that every dismissed civil servant is going to know on his dismissal that he has a right of appeal. Civil servants know that this is a new right of appeal which is being granted and spelled out in the legislation before us.
I hope we would not delay the passage of the measure by having to refer back to the

Civil Service Act
draughtsman so that each section might be contemplated in the light of the principles of interpretation of which I have spoken.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary has just given the most eloquent argument that could possibly have been given in favour of the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Hull. This bill is not one of those casual amendments that are made to legislation from time to time. This is a complete review of the Civil Service Act, the first that has been made for many years. If as the parliamentary secretary has stated this amendment commends itself to him in substance and it is merely a matter of taking a little time to see that this important statute which is the charter of the rights and obligations of public servants is properly drafted, it does not seem to me that that kind of delay is the kind to which there should be any objection whatever.
I feel that the parliamentary secretary should consider very carefully accepting this amendment and if consequential changes are necessary they should be brought forward so that the committee could examine them. It is all very well for the parliamentary secretary to say that the employees will know what their rights are in this matter but if it is such a big job for the draftsman to go through this bill in order to ascertain that it is properly drafted-and he is an eminent lawyer- how is a clerk grade I, if they are still called that, or a messenger expected to know precisely what his rights are?
It seems to me there should be no doubt that the employee will know precisely what his rights are when it is proposed to dismiss him. In the most moderate way possible I urge the government to accept in principle at any rate the amendment moved by my hon. friend, and if there are other consequential amendments to bring them forward to the committee so that we may be absolutely sure that these people whose livelihood it is suggested is going to be taken away from them will be told precisely what their rights are.
The parliamentary secretary and I were in the public service at certain stages of our lives. Probably we did know what our rights were although I must confess I was never very sure of mine. I have known of cases in the past where employees did not in fact know what their rights were. They never had it explained to them. In some instances, through the efflux of time they were unable in fact to exercise the right of appeal. If this happens even once in a decade it is too often. It should not happen at all because of the failure on our part as legislators to put a clear obligation on a deputy head to ensure that these rights are adequately safeguarded.

I am not seeking in any way to be contentious about this but I think my hon. friend from Hull has brought forward a logical amendment soundly based in law and common sense and that it would be in the general interest to accept it.

I find myself in complete agreement with the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I do hope the parliamentary secretary will give some consideration to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hull, particularly in view of what I thought was an extremely moderate and constructive approach to this question by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I can only say that the special committee, which was representative of all parties in this house, gave very careful consideration to this particular point. They consulted the draughtsmen of the bill and they took his opinion in relation to it.
My hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate says that I agree with the amendment. Perhaps I would have to say that the attitude I took was that I had no serious disagreement with the amendment at all but I would suggest, first, that it is unnecessary and, second, it would involve serious delay in the passage of the bill and I would ask the committee not to pass it.

On this question of whether it is unnecessary, I think the parliamentary secretary is over-simplifying things when he says it is not necessary. I do not want to go over the same ground that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate covered with respect to whether or not individuals within the public service know their rights. But I have had some experience in this, having spent some time in the trade union movement where day after day and week after week it is a question of dealing with a collective agreement that might exist. Even in those circumstances, where there is a continual campaign of attempting to acquaint members with their rights under collective agreements, after months and months of discussions of this sort of thing, there are still many employees in industry covered by collective agreements who do not know what their rights are. Surely in an institution such as the public service of Canada, where this sort of educational program and discussion and policing of a collective agreement do not go on, we can expect there will be a higher percentage of people who will not know what are their rights.
Even an individual who fails to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits receives a notification from the commission, and on the notification which says he is disqualified he is told he has the right to appeal within so

many days and he can be represented by a union or anybody else. There is an explanation of what are the rights of an individual even in an unemployment insurance case. Surely it is necessary to have this sort of indication in this clause. If the parliamentary secretary or anyone else says that it would really take up too much time to protect the rights of the individual in this country, I think he is perhaps stretching the reasons for objection a little too much.

Mr. Chairman, may I say a word. I was impressed by what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, but I also feel that the chance of anyone suffering from not knowing what his rights are is so infinitely remote that I am prepared to go along with the decision made by the special committee after serious consideration. This is a day when appeals are in the air and we are all Philadelphia lawyers, and I just do not believe the amendment is necessary.

Before the amendment is put I should like to make one more appeal to the parliamentary secretary. I recognize that he is not a minister. But I would even go so far as to say that since we have a Conservative government I rather regret that he is not a minister, not in our party interests but in the interests of the country.
As I say, I recognize that he is not a minister and that it would be rather embarrassing for him to make a decision on this point off the bat here in the committee this evening. But it does seem to me the point is of sufficient importance, involving as it does a subject very dear to the heart of his leader, namely human rights, that I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary that he let this clause stand and that we go along with the rest of the bill-
No.

-and that we do not seek to rush a matter where human rights may be involved and, in my opinion, are involved, but that we take a few minutes tomorrow after the government has had a chance to look at this and at what the draughting problems are. If they come to the conclusion that, notwithstanding these arguments, they want to go ahead, of course they have a majority and I do not think there will be a filibuster. I am just expressing my personal opinion, but I think that in a matter of this kind, where we want to be non-partisan, where we want to do what is right and fair, the course I am suggesting to the parliamentary secretary is one which I am sure would commend itself to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The blandishments of my hon. friend, coupled as they were with
Civil Service Act
a particular type of kiss which he administered, perhaps may be attractive, and perhaps I would succumb had this not been the subject of deep consideration by the special committee. The special committee having considered it, and having discussed it with the draughtsmen, I venture to suggest that the committee as a whole ought to adopt the clause in its present form.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The question is on the amendment.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 14; nays, 52.
Clause 60 agreed to.
On clause 61-Partisan work prohibited.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make on clause 61 which has to do with political activities. This clause is most objectionable to us. I believe the present section of the act, section 55, deals with the substance of political activity and political partisanship. While section 55 is restrictive, in so far as political activity is concerned, nevertheless it does allow a modicum of political freedom in that in so far as I interpret it-and others have given it the same interpretation-the prohibitions contained therein, in so far as engaging in partisan work is concerned, are confined to the period of an election. I would say that refers to the time between the issuance of a writ and election day. Section 55 does not prohibit an employee in the public service from participating in political activities or from belonging to a political party at times other than during the period of the election. I see the parliamentary secretary looking askance at me. I wonder whether I am talking about the right section.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
Perhaps it was only a look of disagreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Only to indicate that I see very little difference between old section 55 and the present clause 61.

Those were the hon. gentleman's remarks in the special committee as I understood them, Mr. Chairman.
To my way of thinking clause 61 is a complete removal and denial of political freedom and political expression except that the right of the individual to proceed to a polling booth on election day to cast his ballot as he sees fit is protected under the Canada Elections Act. Apart from that this clause removes or emasculates any political expression that the individual might have. At one time within the federal public service, and I suppose in the various provinces of Canada as well, there used to be some connection between

Civil Service Act
employment and political affiliation. I gather that was some years ago. Since the advent of employment by merit and appointment by the civil service commission after competition with other candidates, the sphere of political interference with respect to employment in the public service has lessened. Consequently the degree of restriction on the activities of such employees in the political field should also be lessened.
I think this clause of the bill is directly contrary to our concepts with regard to the expansion of political freedom and the extension of political democracy and also directly contrary to the trend which I understand is taking place in other countries in the world toward extending political freedom and the right of political expression and participation to employees in the service of various governments. As I look at the situation, I would say that no employer or individual who pays the wage or salary of such a person should have the right to dictate to the employee what his activities should be outside the period of time for which he is being paid. We would object to this most strenuously in private industry. If industry in paying wages to an individual attempted to tell him how to vote or how not to vote, what meetings to go to, what party to belong to or to prohibit him from belonging to any party, we would object to this as being an unconscionable act on the part of private industry. Yet we are being asked to do substantially the same thing in this clause. We are being asked to say that an employee in the public service of Canada cannot engage in any political activity, period, apart from casting his ballot on election day.
In my opinion this is contrary to what we consider to be the concepts of the bill of rights which refers to the inherent freedom of speech, freedom of association and assembly. As I read this clause, there is no inherent freedom of speech so far as an employee of the public service of Canada is concerned. He cannot express his opinions on behalf of a candidate for election to the House of Commons, the legislative assembly of a province or the council of either one of the territories.
Under paragraph (b) of subclause 1 the employee is also prohibited from receiving or in any way dealing with any money for the funds of any political party and he is liable to be dismissed if he does so. By virtue of this clause in the bill an individual employed in the public service is denied the right to be a member of a political party, simply a card carrying member, and is also prohibited from contributing financially to a party. Regardless of the denial of the rights of freedom of expression, he is denied that

right. He is even denied the right to subscribe to a publication of a political party, and the clause can be stretched to the extent that he would be denied the right to purchase books published by or promoted and sold by political party agencies. He is perhaps even denied the right to contribute by tossing 50 cents or a dollar into the hat when it is passed at a political meeting because of the prohibition of contributing to the funds of any political party. He may have the right to think, but there is some doubt about that.
Surely we should not be thinking of placing restrictions of this type upon individuals in this day and age just a year or two after we enacted the bill of rights ensuring and enshrining forever the right of freedom of speech and freedom of expression. We should be moving in the other direction in granting these freedoms, rights and responsibilities instead of moving to deny them and to make these people nothing more than units in the public service of Canada. I think this clause should be amended, and the gist of the amendment I intend to move is such as to indicate that we also think there should be some restrictions on such activities.
We say that a person in the public service should be prohibited from engaging in political activity or working on behalf of the election of a candidate during his hours of duty because he is being paid for the work he is performing. We also think that an employee in the public service should be prevented from using property of Her Majesty or of the crown, such as letters, stamps, automobiles or other facilities that may be available to him as a public servant, to advance the cause of any political party. Apart from that, outside his working hours he should have the same fundamental rights and political freedoms as everyone else has in this country. Therefore I move:
That clause 61 be amended by deleting therefrom subclause 1 and substituting therefor the following:
"1. No deputy head or employee shall during his hours of duty engage in partisan work, or at any time use any money, materials, facilities or other property of Her Majesty
(a)	in connection with any election for the election of a member of the House of Commons, a member of the legislature of a province or a member of the council of the Yukon territory or the Northwest Territories, or
(b)	in connection with any form of political activity."

Mr. Chairman, I must indicate at once that I cannot agree with the amendment offered by the hon. member for Skeena. As I read his amendment, it simply provides that a civil servant must devote the time during which he is employed to the work for which he is hired and the second part provides that he must not commit theft.

Surely that is not what the hon. member intended by the amendment, and I am quite sure it is not. If he will look at it again he will notice that it is in the form of preventing a civil servant from using his hours of duty for political party work. Surely he is hired to use his hours of duty for the work of the department and if he is not doing that he is breaking his terms of employment.
As for the second part, which provides that he must not use money, materials or other property of the government in connection with party work, surely he has no right to use government property for his own purposes. That is elementary. It seems to me that the amendment does not express in language the idea that the hon. member was seeking to put forward. As I understood his idea, it was that any prohibition against a civil servant taking part in partisan activity should only apply during his hours of employment. That is my understanding of the position he took.
The old section 55 of the act and the new clause 61 of the bill are, as I read them, in substantially the same language. They are different in form but they are designed for the same purpose. Perhaps it is well that we should read clause 61. It is in these terms:
61. (1) No deputy head or employee shall (a) engage in partisan work in connection with any election for the election of a member of the House of Commons, a member of the legislature of a province or a member of the council of the Yukon territory or the Northwest Territories: or
(b) contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for the funds for any political party.
(2) Every person who violates subsection (1) is liable to be dismissed.
This clause in the bill and its predecessor in the act have been relied on by the civil servants as a protection to them and indeed they have been a useful protection to them through the years. The subject was dealt with in the special committee. There I expressed the idea that my understanding of the interpretation of the words, "engage in partisan work" was that they did not prevent civil servants from actually attending a public political meeting, although I believe that very few of them do so. However, I see nothing in that language which prevents their doing so.
Then I went on to deal with the matter of paying membership fees to a political party. To me it seems that once a civil servant has paid his membership fee to a political party, he has then taken an active step on his part indicating his partisan interests, and similarly if he is collecting funds for the party. In that case, in my view, he has put himself in a position in which his interest as a dues paying member of a political party may be in conflict with his duty as a civil servant; and I take his duty as a civil servant to be
Civil Service Act
to carry out the administrative processes in his particular class of work according to the policies of the government of the day and enacted by parliament, as the case may be. Surely it is a protection to the civil servant that he is not permitted to be put in a position in which his interest is in direct conflict with his duty. As I read the clause and as I have understood it over the years, my observation has been that it has been reasonably effective and that it has accomplished the objective of protecting the service. I should hate to see anything done that would bring civil servants into a position in which they are either in conflict with the duties which they are expected to perform as civil servants or in which they can be reasonably suspect of being in a position in which their personal interest conflicts with their duties as civil servants. My hope would be that nothing would be done in that connection that would bring about such a situation.
There is one other aspect of this matter that concerns me and it is something new that has arisen since the matter was considered in the special committee. The prohibition in clause 61 is with regard to a civil servant engaging in partisan work in connection with the election of a member of the House of Commons and other legislative bodies enumerated and with respect to contributing, receiving or dealing with money for the funds of any political party. There is no prohibition with respect to a civil servant engaging in partisan work in the civil service in connection with a political party which does not have members seeking election to the House of Commons. It is a strange anomaly that has arisen only once to my knowledge, or in one case that I have ever heard of. If he takes care not to contribute funds to that particular party or not to receive or in any way to deal with funds, he is as free as he can be to advocate in an active way the political philosophy he has in mind and to take part in partisan activities. I do not think that sort of thing was ever intended. I think it is purely a case of its never having been thought of.
As the committee and the parliamentary secretary will appreciate, there was the case to which I am referring, namely the case of the Nazi who was a civil servant and who was actively participating in the work of that party, with its many ramifications. This situation is wholly inconsistent with our ideas with respect to a civil servant taking part in partisan activities. Yet not a thing could be effectively done with him under this section. There may be other remedies. It is a rather interesting case. I want to ask the parliamentary secretary whether any examination has been made of that situation since this

Civil Service Act
clause was before the special committee. If so, what conclusion, if any, was arrived at concerning the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Just to answer the last question of the hon. gentleman may I say this. So far as I understand it, no special examination has been undertaken of the provisions of this act having regard to the particular employee and the particular incident to which he refers. The situation with respect to that particular employee has not been related to this section. I am sorry but I cannot give my hon. friend the particulars. May I simply say to him that, with respect to his other remarks, this is one of those occasions on which I agree wholeheartedly with my neighbour and friend.
There is just one thing I should like to bring out. The hon. member who immediately preceded me in speaking seems to have a set of facts much more clearly in his mind than I have them in mine-
That is not unusual.

-with respect to engaging in partisan work under clause (a) of clause 61. What I mean is this. There are many ramifications in connection with what the hon. member said as he went through what he felt constituted partisan work to elect a member of parliament. However, the fact is this. We all know very well that the constitution of every political party states that the people who are members of an association must abide by the constitution of that party which is dedicated to electing as a member to the House of Commons or the legislature, as the case may be, somebody of the particular political colour represented by that party. Do I understand the situation correctly? I really and sincerely feel that this is something with regard to which we would be performing a useful function if we clarify it right here and now. For instance, in my own particular riding may an immigration officer appear publicly at a political meeting and have his picture appear in the local press, let us say, with the executive of a political organization? Is this procedure contravening this article? If it is doing so, may I say it is something that certainly happens in my riding as it might happen in the ridings of other hon. members.
I must say that I quite agree with the hon. member who preceded me in speaking, that this is something that is not clear in the minds of civil servants in particular, the public In general, and perhaps even members of parliament, although I do not know that. We all know that partisan activity or work is involved when we attend political meetings. After all, what are we doing at a political meeting? Are we just sitting there and passing the time of day? No, Mr. Chairman; we are

there organizing to elect candidates of our choice to political office, provincially or federally. I think possibly the hon. member who preceded me has helped to muddy the issue there. We all know very well that is what is involved. May an immigration officer appear publicly at a political meeting, and have his picture in the press supporting a political party? This happened recently in my area. I should like to have an answer to that question. I do not think the hon. member who preceded me has given the answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to say only this. As I understand the situation, there is certainly no restriction upon any civil servant with respect to appearing at a political meeting. However, at such a meeting he has no right, under the existing legislation, to express his views in support of or in opposition to those which are being expressed at that particular time. I mentioned in the committee the incident that occurred many years ago in connection with a customs appraiser in Montreal who went to a Liberal meeting. At the Liberal meeting he interrupted and shouted, "Hourra pour les bleus!" He was immediately thrown out, so he went across to a meeting down the street and there shouted, "Hourra pour les rouges"!" He was thrown out of there and ultimately he was thrown out of his job, although subsequently he was reinstated.
I say that in my own riding political meetings could not be held were it not possible for civil servants to attend such meetings. But for servants to take an active, participating, organizing part would in my opinion-
Or be photographed in the way described by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -or to permit himself to be photographed in the way described by the hon. gentleman, would be improper under this particular clause.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one comment on the question of being photographed at these political meetings. When one considers the words, "engage in partisan work", I think common sense is a pretty good guide. If a man goes to a meeting and happens to be photographed in the body of the meeting, that is not likely to attract much attention; but if he has himself photographed with the executive of a party, I think in common sense that is getting very near engaging in partisan work. He is really aligning himself with a party.
I thought the hon. member for Ottawa West described extremely well the reason for this prohibition. It seems to me that when we use general words about the bill of rights and say that every man must have his rights, we have

to take time off to look at the essentials of the situation. I think all of us realize that when a man is in the civil service, where today he may be working as, say the agent, for want of a better word, of one party one week and a week later he may be the agent of another party, he has to maintain a certain aloofness from both parties.
As I understood it, that was in effect what the hon. member for Ottawa West said, that a man had to maintain an independence which does not apply to any man except one who is engaged in the business of government. When he is engaged in the business of government it seems to me there are certain limitations, which the hon. member for Ottawa West described so well, which inevitably apply to him.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of recapitulating any of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Skeena. I endorse them wholeheartedly. I should like to add, however, that I do not think you will find one newspaper across this country from coast to coast who does not at one time or another cry out about the apathy of the voting public of this country.
We are now being asked in this committee to legislate or to create apathy by statute. We are the greatest single employer in this country and we are ordering by statute all our employees to be apathetic as far as taking an interest in political affairs is concerned.
I realize the parliamentary secretary illustrated what may have been a humourous incident which happened in Montreal regarding the "bleus" and the "rouges", but I should like to give an example of what happens when there is neither a "bleu" nor a "rouge" government in power. In the province of Saskatchewan at the present time there is a civil servant still employed by that government who is sitting as a Liberal member of the opposition. He is drawing his indemnity as a member and also his pay as a civil servant when he is not sitting in session in the legislature. Apparently this has worked out very well so far, so I do not think this bogey that we have heard about is at all worth while.
I think this is something we have built up in our own minds. I worked for some 11 years as a civic servant, which is very similar to being a civil servant; it is a first cousin to a civil servant. Civic employees are not supposed to have any political beliefs, but they have them. They are not supposed to express them, but I called their bluff. I think if we spend time here legislating that the largest group of employees in this country shall not have the same rights as any other
Civil Service Act
employee in this country, we had better take another look at just how democratic we are.
If they are working on political affairs to the detriment of their job, there is a legitimate complaint and they should be reprimanded or dealt with. But once they have done the job they are being paid for, during whatever time they have left, be it on their evenings off, their days off or their holidays, they should have entirely the same rights as any other Canadian living in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I am rather concerned about this particular clause. For clarification I wondered whether this matter could be dealt with. As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, common sense should be used. I quite agree with that. I quite agree that key civil servants should not be taking an active part in politics.
However, there are many mail couriers throughout Canada who refrain from taking any active part in politics because they are afraid they will lose their positions. Mail couriers are today obtaining the job by low tender; it is not a matter of belonging to a political party, yet they are civil servants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, they are not civil servants.

They are afraid of taking any part whatsoever in political meetings because complaints might be made. I wish to ask the parliamentary secretary this question: if they attend a political meeting, can someone complain and are they liable to be removed from that position?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think I should say that a rural mail courier is not a civil servant. He is not governed by this act; he is an independent contractor. As I recollect, a very clear statement was made by the Postmaster General to the house on this subject. He made it clear that when the courier was not engaged in the actual duties of delivering Her Majesty's mail he was not subject in any way to any infringement of his political rights. '

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary may think that the Postmaster General made a very clear statement, but I remember we asked the Postmaster General why the same rule was not applied to public works contractors who, when they are engaged in building a public building, are still allowed to take any part in politics they like without any interference from the government.
Of course, this matter is quite irrelevant to the bill. As the parliamentary secretary has said, these mail couriers are independent contractors, but this usurpation of power by the Postmaster General, with no statutory

Civil Service Act
authority behind it, is something that, having been raised by the hon. member, I think ought to be condemned.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Ottawa West spoke about the amendment as though it meant a civil servant should not loaf on the job or become a thief on the job. We start from the premise that a person has some rights unless they are taken away from him. In my opinion, if this amendment were adopted it would mean that a man has all the political rights and freedoms except when on the job during working hours, and he ought not to use public property in order to engage in this sort of activity. A man maintains those rights unless they are removed, and to this extent the amendment is clear. In effect it removes those rights during working hours and so far as the use of someone else's property is concerned. I cannot follow the reasoning that employees in the public service must not belong to, or support, or indicate any preference for a political party other than that which happens to be in office. This is the reverse of the coin of the argument as given here. Apparently it is all right to be a Tory when the Tories are in office, or a Liberal when the Liberals are in office, but you cannot be a Liberal when the Tories are in office or vice versa.
Nonsense.
Poppycock.

"Nonsense" seems to be the favourite word of some hon. members. But let me follow this through. What, in fact, is being said is that the political convictions of the government in office must filtrate through the entire structure of the civil service.
Irresponsible ballyhoo.
That seems to be a favourite expression of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.
It is the first time I have used it-the first occasion.

Well, it properly expresses his general attitude. If the hon. member disagrees with me, I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will confirm what I have to say. The implication here is that the political complexion of the government in office should filter through the entire structure-that everyone should be neutral politically which, in effect, means agreeing with the political convictions of the government in office. This seems odd to me. Apparently it is all right for the wife of a public servant to be a member and supporter of a political party but it is not all right for the civil servant himself to be so. Apparently it is all right
[Mr. PickersgillJ
for him to have what sympathies he pleases, even though they may be politically contrary to the government in office, but he must not not express them. He can vote, but he cannot join a political party and express views which are contrary to those held by the government in office.
This situation was dealt with in the United Kingdom to some extent through the Whitley council. Though the system which exists over there is not on all fours with the amendment before us tonight, it is in part. In the United Kingdom they have a horizontal division among employees in the public service. Some have complete political freedom-the right to campaign and the like-while others, because of the positions they hold near the top of the administrative ladder, as it were, are prevented from participating in politics in this way because it is felt that their close connection with ministerial activity and authority might create difficulties. Perhaps there would be some sense in our following this line. Let me read a passage from a pamphlet published by the United Kingdom Information Service, Canada, dated January, 1959, called "The British Civil Service". I am reading from page 23 of that publication with respect to the Whitley council as follows:
The government accepted a scheme under which about 62 per cent of the whole civil service (i.e. industrial and non-industrial, in all about one million people) are completely free from restrictions, about 22 per cent are free, subject to ac-aceptance of the need for discretion, to take part in all activities except parliamentary candidature, and 16 per cent remain debarred from national political activities. As many as possible of this last group who wish are given permission to take part in local government and political activities in the local field.
There is this further information:
Any member of the group is completely free of restrictions who intends standing for parliament must resign his appointment before nomination day. If he is not elected to parliament he will, on application within a week of declaration day, be reinstated in his previous capacity. If he is elected, he will be entitled to return to his post provided that:	(a) he ceases to be a member after an
absence not exceeding five years; (b) he had not less than ten years actual service before his election; and (c) he applies for reinstatement within three months of ceasing to be a member.
This is the system which exists in the United Kingdom, a system under which about 62 per cent of the civil service, presumably those in the less responsible administrative posts, have no restrictions placed upon them and are completely free to engage in political activities and to express their political ideas without fear of dismissal or reprisals. It is immaterial whether or not their political views and activities are agreeable to the government in office. So the Whitley council whose recommendations were accepted by

the government, felt that the views expressed by the parliamentary secretary, by the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Ottawa West and others who have spoken about the need for political neutrality and the need for commonsense and discretion in these matters, applied, as far as the United Kingdom is concerned to only some 38 per cent of the civil service, and even some of those were allowed to have a modicum of political freedom subject to discretion as it is here called.
Surely we could easily follow an arrangement of that kind. If it is not agreeable to give complete freedom of political activity and expression, as is proposed in this amendment-I am not too attached to it-then certainly we could devise a proposal which would give some political freedom to people in the lower groups and, in doing so, really take a step toward granting wider political freedom to some individuals.
Amendment negatived: yeas, 3; nays, 53.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I declare the
amendment lost. Shall clause 61 carry?

What we are seeking to do here, if I read the clause correctly is, in effect, to prohibit some employees in the civil service from engaging in partisan work in connection with elections to certain offices while allowing them to engage in partisan work in connection with elections to other types of office, notably municipal councils. These are not mentioned here and I assume, therefore, that there is a right to engage in partisan activity on behalf of candidates for municipal office.
Or even against them.

We know that in some parts of Canada the communist party enters candidates for municipal offices. I am not saying that any member of the civil service would do so, but if he cannot work on behalf of a candidate for a responsible political party is he being put in a position of deciding to work on behalf of a candidate for the communist party in a municipal election? This is precisely what it allows.
(Translation):
In this day of Yom Kippur, when the Jewish religion imposes severe fasting upon its adepts, to expiate their sins, I have agreed to stand in for the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) who is unavoidably absent, and I move in his name the following amendment:
(Text):
That the following proposed amendment be approved by adding to section 61, subsection 1, the following subsection, to be known as (b) immediately after subsection (a), to read as follows:
Civil Service Act
"be a member directly or indirectly of any political party or group in Canada or elsewhere which is known to directly or indirectly advocate discrimination between people because of their race, colour, creed or religion."
And that the present subsection (b) be altered to be known as subsection (c).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have already added in section 33 for the first time a non-discrimination clause. It is the first that has appeared in the Civil Service Act. This represents a step which I am sure met with the unanimous approval of all hon. members of the committee. I think under the circumstances the hon. member's amendment is unnecessary.
Amendment (Mr. Caron) negatived: Yeas, 10; nays, 43.

May I explain that I did not vote on the amendment because a copy was not available to me and I could not follow the rapid reading of it. Section 61 says that no employee should engage in partisan activity. Let us determine the exemptions to this. What people employed in the Canadian public service are free to engage in partisan activity and therefore contribute to political parties and so on even during working hours?
An employee is defined as a person employed in the civil service. In the definition of the words "civil service" it is explained that the reference is to positions in the public service, and certain exceptions are set out. A member of the civil service commission, for instance, can engage in partisan political activities, contribute financially and do whatever he likes. The Clerk of the House of Commons, the Clerk of the Privy Council and of the Senate and the secretary to the Governor General are not to be prohibited from engaging in this type of activity.
They are all deputy heads.
I appreciate that.
Therefore the first part applies.
I appreciate that. I am throwing in everyone I can.
Including many who are not there.

Reference is made to prevailing rate positions. I am sure these are not deputy heads. The annual report of the commission for 1960 indicates that as of September 30 there were 24,172 prevailing rate employees. I assume these are the people referred to in the definition section as holding prevailing rate positions. If that is the case it means there are that many people in the public service who can participate in this type of activity in or out of working hours. I wish to know in what class are

Civil Service Act
salaried employees not under the Civil Service Act? I refer to page 34 of the annual report for 1960 where reference is made to this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That would refer to the national research council, the defence research board and several other organs of the public service as opposed to the civil service.
They would be free to engage in political activity, I take it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not passing an opinion on that. We are dealing only with the act relating to the civil service. While doing so I do not wish to give an interpretation in relation to others who are not within the civil service.
Presumably they are not prohibited by virtue of the provisions of this statute from engaging in political activities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is correct to say they are not prohibited from doing so by virtue of this bill.

They may be prohibited by some other measure, but that is another matter. Certainly prevailing rate employees are not. Reference is made to some 3,000-odd persons described as ship officers and crews who are classed with government railway and ship employees. There are approximately 25,000 people employed in the public service who in my estimation may engage in political activities because they are exempt from the prohibiting clause.
Clause 61 agreed to.
Clause 62 agreed to.
On clause 63-Annual leave.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to move an amendment but I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that there are thousands of employees who are part time employees and who may work three or four hours a day, for instance, in the Post Office Department. These people never have a leave of absence or a holiday. This has been complained about in the house more than once and each time the ministers in question said they would inquire and see if the situation could be remedied.
I referred to a girl who worked for four years in the unemployment insurance office in Montreal without a holiday. She was denied it because it was said she was not a civil servant. There is something wrong somewhere over there, and the parliamentary secretary to the minister should look into the matter to see what can be done. In the
[Mr. Howard.)
big offices in Montreal and Toronto there are thousands of employees working under like conditions who never benefit from any holidays whatsoever in the year. This situation should be corrected. It could be corrected easily if the government would look into the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand the Secretary of State is inquiring into the matter, and I will make a special note to speak to him about it.

I believe there is a clause in the existing act which states in effect that every employee will be granted one and a quarter days leave for every month worked, not to exceed a certain number of days in any one fiscal year. I think the clause is quite clear and there are no exceptions to it in the act. However, when it was put into practice it was found on several occasions I know of that there are regulations or treasury board minutes which supersede the intent of the act. In subclauses 2 and 4 of clause 63 there are these two phrases "as may be prescribed by the regulations" and "subject to the regulations".
I was very interested in what the hon. member for Greenwood said about common sense governing these acts. Unfortunately, apparently the hon. member has not come up against cases such as the rest of us have where common sense is not taken into consideration by officials of those departments. They go by the written rule. The point I am objecting to is that when the regulation becomes more powerful than the act itself a second look should be taken at the regulations, or certain restrictions should be put in them. I would ask the parliamentary secretary to advise us whether under this new clause a civil servant, if he were employed for 11 or 12 months, would be entitled to the full three weeks vacation in any one year, or whether, as it is at the present time, he would be entitled to leave for only six months. Is this the intention of the clause?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder whether my hon. friend's point is not covered by subclause 3 which reads:
No employee shall be granted vacation leave unless he has been employed in the civil service for at least six months.
I do not know that I can give my hon. friend a detailed answer in relation to any particular civil servant or say that the civil servant who has been employed for 10 months and three days is going to have three weeks leave. I think there has to be some type of apportioning of it. I am personally not familiar with the regulations which have existed. I shall be glad to look into it. If my

hon. friend has any complaints in relation to it I shall certainly see that they are drawn to the attention of the commission and of the governor in council when the regulations are being studied and promulgated.
If the employee were employed for seven months would he be entitled to half a year's leave or any leave at all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I of course cannot speak of what the situation may be in the future. Perhaps I can get some advice as to what the situation would be at the present time. My understanding is that he does not earn leave in respect of the first six months of service. He starts to earn leave after he has completed the six months of service and it accumulates from that period on.
In the face of what it says in the existing act, I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary could give us the authority for his not getting leave during the first six months.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My understanding is that there is a treasury board minute based on the recommendation of the civil service commission to that effect. I confess I have not myself seen that document and I would not wish to give any opinion in the House of Commons in respect to it until I had an opportunity personally to study it.
The parliamentary secretary would not give an opinion as to which is the more powerful, the act or the treasury board minute?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would have no doubt of that. As far as the act is concerned it will always govern and the treasury board minute will prevail only if it fails within the four corners of the act.
Clause 63 agreed to.
Clauses 64 to 67, inclusive, agreed to.
On clause 68-Regulations.

I shall skim through clause 68 quickly. Paragraph (o) provides that regulations may be made for the selection, appointment, conditions of employment and remuneration of employees performing duties of a casual, part-time or seasonal nature, notwithstanding anything in the act. Are these employees within the meaning of the definition of employees in the definition section persons employed in the civil service?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes; my understanding is they are employed within the terms of the act but because of the very special nature of the employment, whether it be casual or seasonal, those special regulations do have to
Civil Service Act
be set up, regulations of a type which would not be applicable to the year-round civil servant.

May I have the distinction that is drawn, if there is one, between a casual, part-time or seasonal employee and a prevailing rate employee? Is there a difference in that regard between a casual, part-time or seasonal employee and an employee on a prevailing rate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, I am advised that there is a technical difference between a casual, part-time and seasonal employee that has been a well recognized one. I would be glad to send my hon. friend a memorandum setting forth in detail the distinctions that there are.
Are there distinctions between those people and prevailing rate people, or are they prevailing rate positions? I refer to the casual, part-time and seasonal employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
What we are speaking of here are positions which are established pursuant to the Civil Service Act for casual, part-time and seasonal workers. They have nothing to do with the prevailing rate establishment which, as my hon. friend, knows, is something which is under section 2(l)(b), which is entirely outside the terms of the act. This is for the casual, seasonal or parttime classifications established under the act itself.
Clause 68 agreed to.
Clauses 69 and 70 agreed to.
On clause 71-Ministerial staffs.

This clause deals with
ministerial staffs and the part about which I have some remarks to make has to do with the appointment of executive assistants or private secretaries to a minister to the regular civil service after they have served three years as an executive assistant or private secretary to the minister. The provisions now governing this situation are found in section 61 of the present act and I will read part of section 61. Subsection 1 deals with ministers appointing private secretaries. Subsection 2 reads in part as follows:
...in the event of the minister or other member of the government, oar leader of the opposition for whom he is acting as secretary, ceasing to be a minister or member of the government or to be the leader of the opposition, as the case may be. the said secretary shall thereupon be appointed to a permanent position-
And so on. The new clause corrects certain difficulties that were found to exist in the act as it now stands but it made one change with which I want to concern myself at the moment. There is no longer any requirement

Civil Service Act
that the secretary or executive assistant can only secure this right to be appointed to the regular civil service when the minister ceases to be a minister. It seems to me that provision should be continued in the new legislation. In my view the dropping of that limitation on the right of appointment was an error and can lead to a situation that will be demoralizing to the service without achieving any real purpose in meeting the needs of executive assistants and private secretaries. For that reason I want to put forward an amendment that will have effect of retaining the limitations in that respect in the new clause. I therefore move:
That paragraph' 3 of clause 71 of the bill be amended by adding after the word "minister" in line 27 thereof the following:
"if the minister for whom he is acting as executive assistant or private secretary ceases to be a minister or becomes a minister of another portfolio."
It will be seen that this preserves the former limitation in that respect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In view of the hour I should like to say very briefly that I do not think there is anything I can add to what I said in the special committee and on second reading, and I hope that the committee will not adopt the amendment.
Amendment (Mr. Mcllraith) negatived: Yeas, 10; nays, 46.
Clause 71 agreed to.
Clauses 72 to 85 inclusive agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you recognize the clock, I wonder if I could ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare-it is rather hard to find a minister in the house-what the government proposes we should go ahead with tomorrow and the rest of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, despite what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate says, there seem to be several ministers in the house. Will the estimates continue in that order for the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the intention as of now.
Is it intended to call the Civil Service Act for third reading as the first item tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I would expect so. I really cannot commit the government but I would expect that third reading would be the first item called tomorrow.
